title: Empirical Asset Pricing: A Python Reader’s Companion
text:
Preface
This book aims to provide a reader’s companion to Empirical Asset Pricing: The Cross Section of Stock Returns by Bali, Engle, and Murray (2016) (“BEM”). While I purchased a copy of BEM in 2021, I have never managed to read it in much depth. I think one reason for this is that there is such a tight connection between what is presented in the book and the detailed data analysis underlying it. This means one is inevitably thinking about the details of analysis as one is reading the book and, for me at least, wishing that one could run the code while reading the book. Unfortunately, the authors do not provide the source code they used to generate the tables and charts in the book.
With this book, I aim to fill the gap left by BEM by providing code to reproduce every analysis contained in BEM.1 This book largely follows Bali et al. (2016).
Part I introduces the core ideas using the 1988–2012 “methodologies sample” of Bali et al. (2016). 1  Preliminaries also discusses the software packages used to run the analysis included herein, including the production of tables and charts.
Part II provides the core empirical analyses of Bali et al. (2016) starting with the construction of the CRSP sample and estimation of market betas before moving on to examine various dimensions studied in prior research on the cross-section of stock returns.

title: Empirical Asset Pricing: A Python Reader’s Companion
text:
Why Python Polars?
My goal here is to allow readers to open the code behind a table, rerun it in a notebook, and change a breakpoint, a sample screen, or a factor model. My hope is that you can carry the workflow I use here into your own research. The software is freely available.2 Reproducing the results requires access to the relevant data from Wharton Research Data Services (WRDS, pronounced “words”).
Having chosen Python, one also needs to choose a data frame library. While pandas has been the default data frame library for Python users since about 2012, when it was really the only such library, Python Polars seems to be the better choice in 2026. With ideas such as lazy data frames and expressions, Polars can process large amounts of data more quickly and with fewer computing resources than pandas can. Python Polars has syntax that is often more intuitive for humans than pandas. If you are new to Polars, or even new to Python, Chapter 2 of the Python Polars edition of Empirical Research in Accounting: Tools and Methods provides a fast-paced introduction to the basic ideas.
With Python Polars, pretty much every analysis in the book can be run in seconds. Even if you are using AI agents to run your analysis, you will appreciate the performance offered by Python Polars, as you will spend less time waiting for output and have less concern that your AI is going to use up all the RAM on your computer.
More information about how to set up your computer to run the analyses in this book is provided in Data.




Bali, Turan G., Robert F. Engle, and Scott Murray. 2016. Empirical Asset Pricing: The Cross Section of Stock Returns. John Wiley & Sons. https://www.wiley.com/en-us/empirical-asset-pricing-the-cross-section-of-stock-returns-p-9781118095041.

title: 1  Preliminaries
text:
1.1 Data
The primary data source for the analysis in Bali et al. (2016) is CRSP. Bali et al. (2016) discuss several ways of obtaining CRSP data that applied in 2016 before indicating that they obtained CRSP data in form of SAS data accessed on WRDS servers using SSH (Bali et al. 2016, 104).
I store the WRDS tables used in this book as Parquet files.

title: 1  Preliminaries
text:
1.1.1 WRDS tables
In 2016, when Bali et al. (2016) was published, the canonical form of WRDS data was SAS data files. For users with WRDS access, my wrds2pg package can be use to generate Parquet files from SAS data files. However, I recommend getting data from the WRDS PostgreSQL server instead.
Since 2017, WRDS has provided data through a PostgreSQL database server. As discussed in Gow and Ding (2024), the SAS data files and the PostgreSQL server can be viewed as canonical sources of WRDS data. For users with WRDS access, my db2pq package can be used to generate Parquet files from the PostgreSQL database. Because using db2pq is faster and more robust than using wrds2pg, I recommend that you use db2pq.
Some books and code repositories reduce the quantity of data retrieved from WRDS by taking subsets of observations or variables. For example, Tidy Finance (Scheuch et al. 2024) use a script to download a selection of variables from the CRSP daily stock file for subsets of firms in batches. In contrast, I download the full tables in each case.
While downloading the full WRDS data files used here can take several minutes even with a fast internet connection, I think this is a cost worth bearing for several reasons. First, many finance researchers will only have access to annual updates and will use the data on a near-daily basis. So the fixed cost of downloading the data can be amortized over many uses.
Second, managing vintages of data is much easier with the approach used here. The core db2pq function wrds_update_pq() used below retains information about the vintage of the data on WRDS and this avoids downloading data that is of the same vintage as the user already has. Other functions offered by db2pq allow the user to retain older vintages and swap them easily if one wants to reproduce data using a specific vintage.
It seems not uncommon for researchers to get a certain set of variables in initial analysis, then need to go back to retrieve additional variables later on when the vintage of the data might be different. In such cases, a research is confronted with a choice of updating all variables, potentially losing finely balanced results in the process, or just getting data for the additional variables, which introduces potential inconsitencies in the data. By getting all variables at the outset, this issue is avoided.
Another reason to get the full data files relates to reproducibility. If your results are generated on a specific subset of a WRDS data file, then I need to get that specific subset to reproduce them. Because researchers often do not include the code to produce the WRDS data files they use, additional frictions are introduce to reproducibiliy in practice. In contrast, using crsp.dsf produced using db2pq will produce exactly the same results as I’d get from using crsp.dsf in the PostgreSQL database.
A third approach to managing data avoids storing local data at all. For example, Gow and Ding (2024) provide code to run analyses in their book using direct connections to the WRDS PostgreSQL server with little or no persistence of data locally. While this does reduce the initial set-up costs, it introduces issues of performance and even reproducibility that do not seem worth forgoing the modest initial setup costs of the approach used here.1

1.1.1.1 Compustat (comp)
Compustat is the most common source of financial-statement data for academic research, particulary for US firms. Academic researchers generally get Compustat data through WRDS.
While Compustat is a rich source of data from income statement, balance sheets, and cash flow statements, its direct use by Bali et al. (2016) is limited to calculating the book value of common equity. The table from Compustat needed for this purpose is comp.funda, which supplies annual data.
More on Compustat can be found in Chapter 6 and Chapter 8 of Gow and Ding (2024).
While Bali et al. (2016) make little use of Compustat data, many studies of the cross-section of stock returns go deeper into financial statements. Chapter 14 of Gow and Ding (2024) covers Bernard and Thomas (1989), which uses quarterly income before extraordinary items (ibq in comp.fundq) to measure earnings surprises, then compare abnormal returns across earnings-surprise deciles after the announcements. Chapter 15 of Gow and Ding (2024) focuses on Sloan (1996), which uses annual financial statements (comp.funda) to separate earnings into accrual and cash-flow components, then compares subsequent returns across portfolios sorted on accruals.


1.1.1.2 CRSP (crsp)
The primary source of data in Bali et al. (2016) is the CRSP database. According to its website, “the Center for Research in Security Prices, LLC (CRSP) maintains the most comprehensive collection of security price, return, and volume data for the NYSE, AMEX and NASDAQ stock markets. Additional CRSP files provide stock indices, beta-based and cap-based portfolios, treasury bond and risk-free rates, mutual funds, and real estate data. [CRSP] maintains the most comprehensive collection of security price, return, and volume data for the NYSE, AMEX and NASDAQ stock markets. Additional CRSP files provide stock indices, beta-based and cap-based portfolios, treasury bond and risk-free rates, mutual funds, and real estate data.”
According to WRDS, “CRSP contains end-of-day and month-end prices on all listed NYSE, Amex, and NASDAQ common stocks along with basic market indices, and includes the most comprehensive distribution information available, with the most accurate total return calculations.”
In 2022, CRSP introduced a new data format called CIZ.2 The CIZ format replaced the SIZ format available when Bali et al. (2016) was written. CRSP stopped releasing SIZ format data in early 2025, so no data on returns and stock prices are available in the SIZ format for periods after 2024.
One major change with CIZ was to the layout of the tables, with CIZ tables often being much larger because they contain data from what were multiple tables in SIZ.3
A second change with CIZ affected the calculation of monthly returns. With SIZ, monthly returns are calculated from month-end to month-end, with dividends reinvested at month-end. In contrast, CIZ compounds daily returns over the month, with dividends reinvested on their ex-dividend dates.4
A third change with CIZ was the incorporation of any applicable delisting returns into the reported monthly return. In contrast, the SIZ data available to Bali et al. (2016) placed delisting returns in a separate table and researchers bore the burden of incorporating delisting returns, which were often missing from that table. See CRSP’s comparison of the formats.
Because my focus here is on providing a reader’s companion to Bali et al. (2016), I use the final vintage of the SIZ data throughout this version of the book. Because the SIZ files I use come from a later CRSP vintage than used in BEM, the underlying data can still differ, though in practice not by much. A later edition of this book may instead use CIZ data or provide a guide to how the analyses could be conducted using CIZ data.
Daily returns come from crsp.dsf and monthly returns from crsp.msf. We use crsp.msenames for data on industries and the exchanges on which stocks are traded. Delisting returns come from crsp.msedelist and index data from crsp.msi.
The final CRSP table we use is crsp.ccmxpf_lnkused. CRSP provides PERMNO, its own “permanent identifier” for each security in its database. Additionally, CRSP provides a company-level identifier, PERMCO, for each company. WRDS tells us that CRSP’s goals in creating these identifiers are to allow “for clean and accurate backtesting, time-series and event studies, measurement of performance, accurate benchmarking, and securities analysis.” Howver, the firm identifier on Compustat is GVKEY and crsp.ccmxpf_lnkused provides a way to link CRSP data with the relevant Compustat records. Chapter 7 of Gow and Ding (2024) explains how to link CRSP and Compustat.5


1.1.1.3 Fama-French factors (ff)
I use two WRDS tables, ff.factors_monthly and ff.factors_daily, for the Fama–French factors and the risk-free rate in many of the analyses. For example, the beta chapter uses the market excess return from both tables to estimate daily and monthly betas.
For some replications I use archived releases from Kenneth French’s Data Library to get closer to the factor vintages available when BEM prepared their book. The skewness, idiosyncratic volatility, and liquid samples chapters use the June 2014 release. The four-factor volatility model also uses the daily momentum series from that release. eap_pl.get_ff_factors() retrieves a specified vintage and keeps a checksum-verified local copy for later renders.


1.1.1.4 Source vintages
Table 1.1 lists the inputs used in this build. The source update date comes from the metadata embedded in each Parquet file, read with db2pq. It is not the sample end date or the date the file was downloaded.



Code
import re

from db2pq import pq_last_modified
from IPython.display import Markdown, display

tables = [
    ("comp", "funda", "Compustat",
     "Annual fundamentals for book equity."),
    ("crsp", "dsf", "CRSP legacy (SIZ)",
     "Daily returns for beta estimation in @sec-bem-beta and daily prices, returns, and volume for @sec-liquidity-replication."),
    ("crsp", "msf", "CRSP legacy (SIZ)",
     "Legacy prices, shares outstanding, and monthly returns."),
    ("crsp", "msenames", "CRSP legacy (SIZ)",
     "Historical share codes, exchanges, and industries."),
    ("crsp", "msedelist", "CRSP legacy (SIZ)",
     "Delisting returns and codes for monthly holding-period returns."),
    ("crsp", "msi", "CRSP legacy (SIZ)",
     "CRSP value-weighted index for the market factor comparison."),
    ("crsp", "ccmxpf_lnkused", "CRSP/Compustat Merged",
     "Historical links from Compustat firms to CRSP securities."),
    ("ff", "factors_monthly", "Fama–French",
     "Monthly factors and the risk-free rate for betas, alphas, and market checks."),
    ("ff", "factors_daily", "Fama–French",
     "Daily market excess returns for the crash checks in @sec-bem7-market and for estimating daily betas."),
]

rows = [
    "| WRDS table | Dataset | Used for | Source updated |",
    "|:---|:---|:---|:---|",
]
for schema, name, dataset, purpose in tables:
    metadata = pq_last_modified(name, schema) or ""
    match = re.search(r"Updated (\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})", metadata)
    updated = match[1] if match else "Not recorded"
    rows.append(f"| `{schema}.{name}` | {dataset} | {purpose} | {updated} |")

display(Markdown("\n".join(rows)))

1.1.1.5 Create the Parquet repository
Copy .env.example to .env in the book checkout and set DATA_DIR to your Parquet root and WRDS_ID to your WRDS username. After uv sync, run the setup script from that checkout. If you already have the source files there, you can skip this step. If your WRDS account lacks access to the legacy CRSP tables, use licensed SIZ extracts at the corresponding paths. eap_pl.load_parquet() reads these files from DATA_DIR/schema/table.parquet.
uv run scripts/download_wrds_tables.py
The following Python example shows how the script uses db2pq.wrds_update_pq() to export the WRDS tables to DATA_DIR.
from db2pq import wrds_update_pq
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

tables = {
    "crsp": ["msf", "dsf", "msenames", "msedelist", "msi", "ccmxpf_lnkused"],
    "comp": ["funda"],
    "ff": ["factors_monthly", "factors_daily"],
}

for schema, names in tables.items():
    for name in names:
        wrds_update_pq(name, schema)



1.1.2 Other data sources
The annual methods chapters construct December betas, size, and book-to-market from the local source data when needed. See Chapters 8, 9, and 10 for how each measure is constructed. The monthly replications estimate the 12-month daily beta on demand with eap_pl.load_monthly_betas(). See the render instructions.
The size builder and the CRSP and Value chapters use the BLS all-items CPI for urban consumers, not seasonally adjusted, from FRED, to express market capitalizations in December 2012 dollars. This file does not come from WRDS.
Chapter 13 uses the December 2013 Pástor–Stambaugh liquidity release bundled with eap_pl.

title: 1  Preliminaries
text:
1.2 Winsorization and Truncation
Winsorization caps values outside chosen percentile cutoffs at the corresponding cutoff. Truncation sets those values to missing, so analyses that require the variable exclude those observations. In Section 1.2, Bali et al. (2016) describe both methods as ways to limit the influence of extreme values. They suggest capping observations that still convey information about genuinely high or low values, and consider truncation when the extremes appear to come from a different process. They urge caution when the conclusions depend on which treatment is used.
BEM compute the cutoffs separately for each year or month because they analyze each period’s cross-section before summarizing the results over time. Their 0.5% rule uses the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles. In Chapter 3, both variables are winsorized for Pearson correlations, and Spearman correlations use ranks of the original values. In Chapter 6, the regressors are winsorized and the excess-return outcome is used as observed.
I compute the winsorization cutoffs by linear interpolation with .eap.winsorize(prob=0.005, quantile_method="linear"). The eap_pl.winsorized_corr() helper applies this rule to each variable after keeping pairs with two finite values. In Chapter 8, .over("month") computes cutoffs separately for each month’s beta estimates. I then fit the Fama–MacBeth regressions with statspai.fama_macbeth().
For examples of winsorization and truncation and a comparison with robust regression, see Chapter 24 of Empirical Research in Accounting.

title: 1  Preliminaries
text:
1.3 Newey and West (1987) Adjustment
In Section 1.3, Bali et al. (2016) explain why inference on a time-series mean can be sensitive to changing variance and correlation across periods. Regressing a series on a constant gives its sample mean as the intercept. The adjustment of Newey and West (1987) estimates the standard error using covariances across periods, with less weight on more distant lags. Depending on the pattern of autocorrelation, the adjustment can increase or decrease the standard error. In Chapter 5, BEM use the adjustment for average portfolio returns and spreads, and in time-series factor regressions for portfolio alphas.
For Fama–MacBeth regressions, BEM apply the adjustment to the sequence of estimated coefficients, with one estimate per cross-section. BEM motivate six lags with a rule of thumb for a series of about 600 monthly observations and also use six lags in their annual example, which has only 24 coefficient estimates. Gow et al. (2010) call this procedure FM-NW and find that its standard errors can remain too small when the underlying panel has both cross-sectional and time-series dependence. A short coefficient series provides limited information about persistence in the underlying data (Gow et al. 2010, 488).
The annual, beta, size, and book-to-market regressions replicated here use realized excess returns over nonoverlapping holding periods. This resembles the return-based application in Gow et al. (2010, sec. V), where shared shocks across stocks are the main concern. For slope inference, the relevant serial dependence involves the joint behavior of regressors and residuals. Size is highly persistent in my replications. Across specifications, the pooled lag-one correlations between residuals for the same stock range from about \(-0.05\) to \(-0.01\).
For every slope in the monthly replications, the ordinary and six-lag tests agree at the 5% level. Section 6.2 shows how the adjustment changes inference on size in the annual example.
For more on Newey–West, Fama–MacBeth, and clustering, see Section 5.6 of Empirical Research in Accounting in the StatsPAI edition or the Polars edition.

title: 1  Preliminaries
text:
1.4 Python packages

1.4.1 Polars
I use Polars, imported as pl, to filter, join, and summarize the data throughout the book. A DataFrame holds the data in memory, and a LazyFrame describes a query that runs when I call .collect(). Expressions such as pl.col("ret") refer to columns, and .over("month") applies a calculation separately within each month. See the Polars user guide.


1.4.2 eap_pl
Here eap stands for “Empirical Asset Pricing” and pl is the standard abbreviation for Polars. The eap_pl package was created specifically for this reader’s companion and streamlines work that recurs across chapters, including reading local Parquet tables, constructing stock-level variables, and forming portfolios.
Importing eap_pl also registers the .eap namespace for Polars expressions and DataFrames. For example, .eap.winsorize() clips an expression at quantile cutoffs. For more details, see the eap_pl function reference.


1.4.3 Great Tables
I use Great Tables to format the book’s tables, usually through .eap.show_table() on a Polars DataFrame. For tables that need grouped rows or spanning column headings, I use Great Tables methods through .style, as in the table of beta portfolio alphas and factor loadings. See the Great Tables documentation.


1.4.4 plotnine_polars
I use plotnine_polars for all figures in the book. It adds .ggplot() to Polars DataFrames and lets me build figures by adding layers, scales, and labels using plotnine’s grammar of graphics. The figures on the composition of the CRSP sample show how this works with time series grouped by exchange or industry. See the plotnine_polars documentation.


1.4.5 StatsPAI
I use StatsPAI (statspai) to estimate regressions and calculate standard errors. For example, statspai.fama_macbeth() fits a cross-sectional regression in each period, averages the coefficients over time, and can apply a Newey–West adjustment to the standard errors of those averages. The Fama–MacBeth chapter shows this for annual data. See the StatsPAI project page.

title: 2  Summary Statistics
text:
2.1 Implementation
In Chapter 2, Bali et al. (2016) summarize the distribution of stock characteristics within each year, then average those statistics across years. This gives each year’s cross-section equal weight.

title: 2  Summary Statistics
text:
2.1.1 Periodic Cross-Sectional Summary Statistics
The methodologies sample (Bali et al. 2016, sec. 1.1) covers US common stocks at each December 31 from 1988 through 2012. I take the December value of the 12-month daily beta from Chapter 8. It uses all available daily excess returns in the calendar year and requires at least 200 matched observations.

import polars as pl

from eap_pl import build_annual_panel, load_annual_betas

annual_beta = load_annual_betas().collect()

For each year, compute the statistics across the stocks with a beta. I use the sample standard deviation, bias-adjusted skewness and excess kurtosis, and linearly interpolated percentiles. The count is the number of available values in that cross-section.

def cross_section(variable):
    x = pl.col(variable)
    return [
        x.mean().alias("Mean"),
        x.std().alias("SD"),
        x.skew(bias=False).alias("Skew"),
        x.kurtosis(fisher=True, bias=False).alias("Kurt."),
        x.min().alias("Min"),
        x.quantile(.05, interpolation="linear").alias("5%"),
        x.quantile(.25, interpolation="linear").alias("25%"),
        x.median().alias("Median"),
        x.quantile(.75, interpolation="linear").alias("75%"),
        x.quantile(.95, interpolation="linear").alias("95%"),
        x.max().alias("Max"),
        x.count().alias("n"),
    ]

annual_stats = (
    annual_beta.group_by("year")
    .agg(cross_section("Beta"))
    .sort("year")
)

title: 2  Summary Statistics
text:
2.2 Presentation and Interpretation
I also summarize year-end market capitalization in millions of dollars, its natural logarithm (size), book-to-market, and the following calendar year’s excess return. build_annual_panel() assembles these observations using start_year and end_year, which default to 1988 and 2012.
The December beta observations already calculated for Table 2.1 define the stock-years in the panel. The helper uses permno and formation year as the join keys. build_sizes() provides December market capitalization and its log, as described in Chapter 9. build_book_to_market() supplies the ratio of prior-year fiscal book equity to prior December market capitalization, as described in Chapter 10. I use its signed ratio, consistent with the negative observations in BEM Table 2.3.
betas = annual_betas.lazy().filter(pl.col("year").is_between(start_year, end_year))
keys = ["permno", "year"]
sizes = build_sizes()
capitalizations = (
    sizes.lazy()
    .filter(pl.col("month").dt.month() == 12)
    .select("permno", year=pl.col("month").dt.year(), MktCap="cap", Size="log_cap")
    .filter(pl.col("year").is_between(start_year, end_year))
)
book_to_market = (
    build_book_to_market(sizes).lazy()
    .filter(pl.col("month").dt.month() == 12)
    .select("permno", year=pl.col("month").dt.year(), BM="bm_raw")
    .filter(pl.col("year").is_between(start_year, end_year))
)
For each stock and holding year, the helper compounds the available monthly returns reported by CRSP. BEM §1.1 does not spell out how its annual returns handle delistings. The helper compounds the monthly risk-free returns separately, requiring 12 observations for the year.
stock_returns = (
    load_parquet("msf", "crsp")
    .filter(
        pl.col("date").is_between(pl.date(start_year + 1, 1, 1), pl.date(end_year, 12, 31)),
        pl.col("ret").is_finite(),
    )
    .with_columns(year=pl.col("date").dt.year())
    .group_by(keys)
    .agg(gross_stock=(1 + pl.col("ret")).product())
)
risk_free = (
    load_parquet("factors_monthly", "ff")
    .with_columns(year=pl.col("date").dt.year())
    .filter(pl.col("year").is_between(start_year + 1, end_year))
    .group_by("year")
    .agg(gross_rf=(1 + pl.col("rf")).product(), n=pl.col("rf").count())
    .filter(pl.col("n") == 12)
)
Subtract the annual risk-free return from the stock return and express the difference in percentage points. Subtracting one from the holding year aligns the return with the characteristics measured the preceding December. For example, the return earned in 1989 is joined to the stock’s 1988 characteristics.
next_year = (
    stock_returns.join(risk_free, on="year", validate="m:1")
    .select(
        "permno",
        year=pl.col("year") - 1,
        excess=100 * (pl.col("gross_stock") - pl.col("gross_rf")),
    )
)
The left joins keep each stock-year in the beta sample even when a characteristic or return is missing. end_year is both the last formation year and the last calendar year included in the return calculations. In the default sample, this leaves the 2012 formation rows with missing next-year returns. The final .collect() returns the assembled panel as a Polars DataFrame.
return (
    betas.join(capitalizations, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(book_to_market, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(next_year, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .collect()
)

annual_panel = build_annual_panel(annual_betas=annual_beta)

Apply the same summary to each variable separately. This keeps stocks with a beta but no book-to-market ratio in the beta row. The observation count reflects the available data for each variable.

    annual_panel.unpivot(on=variables, index="year", variable_name="Measure")
    .group_by("year", "Measure")
    .agg(cross_section("value"))
    .group_by("Measure")
    .agg(pl.exclude("year", "Measure").mean())
)

3.1 Implementation
In Chapter 3, Bali et al. (2016) compare the cross-sectional associations among beta, size, book-to-market, and next-year excess return. I use the 1988–2012 annual panel from Chapter 2.

title: 3  Correlation
text:
3.1.1 Periodic Cross-Sectional Correlations
For variables \(X\) and \(Y\) in year \(t\), keep the \(n_t\) stocks for which both variables are observed. The Pearson correlation measures linear association. With \(\bar X_t\) and \(\bar Y_t\) denoting the means in this paired cross-section, the correlation is
\[
\rho_t(X,Y)=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_t}(X_{i,t}-\bar X_t)(Y_{i,t}-\bar Y_t)}
{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n_t}(X_{i,t}-\bar X_t)^2}
\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n_t}(Y_{i,t}-\bar Y_t)^2}}.
\tag{3.1}\]
For the Pearson entries in Table 3.1, winsorize each variable at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles of the paired cross-section before computing its mean and correlation.
The Spearman correlation measures association between ranks. Let \(x_{i,t}\) and \(y_{i,t}\) be the ranks of the original values within the paired cross-section, with rank 1 assigned to the smallest value. When neither variable has ties, the rank difference \(d_{i,t}=x_{i,t}-y_{i,t}\) gives
\[
\rho_t^S(X,Y)=1-\frac{6\sum_{i=1}^{n_t}d_{i,t}^2}{n_t(n_t^2-1)}.
\tag{3.2}\]
With ties, give equal values their average rank and compute the Pearson correlation of the two rank vectors. This is the calculation used by pl.corr(method="spearman"), including when Equation 3.2 applies.

from eap_pl import correlation_matrix, period_correlations

Average the annual coefficients for each pair. If \(\mathcal T_{XY}\) is the set of years with an available coefficient and \(N_{XY}\) is its size, the Pearson and Spearman averages are

\[
\bar\rho^S(X,Y)=\frac{1}{N_{XY}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_{XY}}\rho_t^S(X,Y).
\tag{3.4}\]

3.2 Interpreting Correlations
The two companion figures plot the annual coefficients in Table 3.1. Each panel uses formation years on the horizontal axis. In the second figure, the return paired with year \(t\) comes from year \(t+1\).


Code
from plotnine_polars import aes

def plot_correlations(pairs):
    labels = [f"{variables[a]} and {variables[b]}" for a, b in pairs]
    correlations = pl.concat(
        annual.select("year", Pearson=f"Pearson {a}–{b}", Spearman=f"Spearman {a}–{b}")
        .unpivot(index="year", variable_name="method", value_name="correlation")
        .with_columns(pair=pl.lit(label))
        for (a, b), label in zip(pairs, labels, strict=True)
    ).with_columns(pl.col("pair").cast(pl.Enum(labels)))
    return (
        correlations
        .ggplot(aes(x="year", y="correlation", color="method", linetype="method"))
        .geom_hline(yintercept=0, color="#b3b3b3", size=0.4)
        .geom_line(na_rm=True)
        .facet_wrap("pair", ncol=1)
        .scale_x_continuous(breaks=range(1988, 2013, 4))
        .scale_color_manual(values={"Pearson": "#24639a", "Spearman": "#ac4c27"})
        .scale_linetype_manual(values={"Pearson": "solid", "Spearman": "dashed"})
        .labs(x="Formation year", y="Correlation", color="", linetype="")
        .theme_minimal()
        .add_theme(figure_size=(8, 6), legend_position="top")
    )

title: 4  Persistence Analysis
text:
4.1 Implementation
In Chapter 4, Bali et al. (2016) measure persistence by correlating a stock characteristic with its own future value across stocks. I use the December 1988–2012 panel from Chapter 2, including its signed book-to-market ratio.

title: 4  Persistence Analysis
text:
4.1.1 Periodic Cross-Sectional Persistence
For a lag of \(\tau\) years, match stocks by permno in years \(t\) and \(t+\tau\). For each characteristic \(X\), keep the set \(\mathcal S_{t,\tau}\) of stocks with finite values of \(X\) in both years. Within this matched sample, winsorize each year’s values separately at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles. Using the winsorized values and their cross-sectional means, the Pearson correlation is
\[
\rho_{t,t+\tau}(X)=
\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_{t,\tau}}
      (X_{i,t}-\bar X_t)(X_{i,t+\tau}-\bar X_{t+\tau})}
     {\displaystyle\sqrt{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_{t,\tau}}(X_{i,t}-\bar X_t)^2}
                   \sqrt{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_{t,\tau}}(X_{i,t+\tau}-\bar X_{t+\tau})^2}}.
\tag{4.1}\]
Shift the future year’s join key back by the lag so that each stock’s observation in \(t+\tau\) joins its observation in \(t\). Use the same winsorized Pearson correlation as in Chapter 3.

from eap_pl import winsorized_corr

measures = ["Beta", "Size", "BM"]
lags = range(1, 6)
characteristics = annual_panel.select("permno", "year", *measures)

def annual_persistence(lag):
    future = characteristics.with_columns(year=pl.col("year") - lag)
    return (
        characteristics.join(future, on=["permno", "year"], suffix="_future", validate="1:1")
        .group_by("year")
        .agg(
            winsorized_corr(pl.col(x), pl.col(f"{x}_future")).fill_nan(None).alias(x)
            for x in measures
        )
        .with_columns(pl.lit(lag).alias("Lag"))
    )

annual = pl.concat([annual_persistence(lag) for lag in lags]).sort("Lag", "year")

)

4.1.2 Average Cross-Sectional Persistence
Give each formation year equal weight. With \(N\) years indexed from 1 through \(N\), the average persistence at lag \(\tau\) is
\[
\rho_\tau(X)=\frac{1}{N-\tau}\sum_{t=1}^{N-\tau}\rho_{t,t+\tau}(X).
\tag{4.2}\]
Here \(N=25\), so the one-year estimate averages 24 correlations and the five-year estimate averages 20. Table 4.2 reports the averages for beta and Table 4.3 puts all three characteristics side by side.

title: 4  Persistence Analysis
text:
4.2 Interpreting Persistence
Low beta persistence can reflect changing market exposures, noisy estimates, or both. Overlapping estimation windows can raise the correlation because the two estimates use some of the same returns. Here the December 12-month betas use daily returns from separate calendar years. The set of stocks with valid measurements at both dates can also change with the lag, so differences across lags reflect both the time between measurements and the stocks observed at both dates.

5.1 Univariate Portfolio Analysis
In Chapter 5, Bali et al. (2016) use portfolio sorts to study how next year’s excess return varies with beta, market capitalization, and book-to-market. I form portfolios at each December year-end from 1988 to 2012 using the panel from Chapter 2. Holding returns run from 1989 to 2012.

title: 5  Portfolio Analysis
text:
5.1.1 Breakpoints
In year \(t\), let \(\{X_t\}\) be the available values of the sort variable and \(p_k\) the probability used for breakpoint \(k\). For \(n_P\) portfolios, calculate \(n_P-1\) breakpoints.
\[
B_{k,t}=\operatorname{Pctl}_{p_k}(\{X_t\}).
\tag{5.1}\]
The beta sort uses the 10th, 20th, 40th, 60th, 80th, and 90th percentiles. The first and last groups each hold about a tenth of the stocks, giving a closer look at both tails of the distribution. I use linear interpolation for the percentiles.

def breakpoints(stocks, variable, probabilities, by):
    return stocks.group_by(by).agg(
        pl.col(variable).quantile(p, interpolation="linear").alias(f"{p:.0%}")
        for p in probabilities
    )

5.1.2 Portfolio Formation
With \(B_{0,t}=-\infty\) and \(B_{n_P,t}=\infty\), portfolio \(k\) contains
\[
P_{k,t}=\{i:B_{k-1,t}\le X_{i,t}\le B_{k,t}\}.
\tag{5.2}\]
Both endpoints are included, as in BEM. A stock exactly on a breakpoint can enter both adjacent portfolios. The code joins each stock to its year’s breakpoint intervals, then keeps the intervals that contain its sort value.

from itertools import pairwise

def form_portfolios(stocks, variable, breaks, by, label):
    cutoffs = [pl.col(column) for column in breaks.columns if column not in by]
    edges = [pl.lit(-float("inf")), *cutoffs, pl.lit(float("inf"))]
    intervals = pl.concat([
        breaks.select(*by, pl.lit(group).alias(label), lower=lower, upper=upper)
        for group, (lower, upper) in enumerate(pairwise(edges), 1)
    ])
    return (
        stocks.join(intervals, on=by)
        .filter(pl.col(variable).is_between("lower", "upper"))
        .drop("lower", "upper")
    )

beta_members = form_portfolios(beta_stocks, "Beta", beta_breaks, ["year"], "portfolio")

5.1.3 Average Portfolio Values
For an available outcome \(Y\) and weight \(W\), the portfolio outcome is
\[
Y_{k,t}=\frac{\sum_{i\in P_{k,t}} W_{i,t}Y_{i,t}}
              {\sum_{i\in P_{k,t}} W_{i,t}}.
\tag{5.3}\]
Here \(Y_{i,t}\) is the stock’s excess return in year \(t+1\). For equal weights use \(W_{i,t}=1\). For value weights use December market capitalization and calculate the numerator and denominator on the same set of stocks with available returns and weights. For each year, form the high-minus-low spread
\[
Y_{\mathrm{Diff},t}=Y_{n_P,t}-Y_{1,t}.
\tag{5.4}\]

portfolio_columns = [str(group) for group in range(1, 8)]
univariate_columns = [*portfolio_columns, "7–1"]
last_holding_year = 2012

def univariate_series(cells, outcome):
    return (
        cells.pivot(on="portfolio", index="year", values=outcome)
        .sort("year")
        .select("year", *portfolio_columns, (pl.col("7") - pl.col("1")).alias("7–1"))
    )

r = pl.col("excess")
valid = pl.all_horizontal(r.is_finite(), pl.col("MktCap").is_finite())
w = pl.col("MktCap").filter(valid)
beta_returns = (
    beta_members.filter(pl.col("year") < last_holding_year)
    .group_by("year", "portfolio")
    .agg(EW=r.mean(), VW=(w * r.filter(valid)).sum() / w.sum())
    .with_columns(pl.col("VW").fill_nan(None))
)
beta_ew = univariate_series(beta_returns, "EW")
beta_vw = univariate_series(beta_returns, "VW")

Average the portfolio outcomes and the spreads across the \(T\) available holding years.
\[

Regress each annual portfolio return on factors from the same holding year. The market model, Fama–French three-factor model, and Carhart four-factor model are
\[

\tag{5.7}\]

text:
5.2 Bivariate Independent-Sort Analysis

5.2.1 Breakpoints
To study returns across market-cap groups while controlling for beta, keep stocks with both characteristics. For an independent sort, calculate both sets of breakpoints across this same cross-section. Let \(j\) index the \(n_1\) groups of \(X_1\) and \(k\) index the \(n_2\) groups of \(X_2\).
\[
B_{1j,t}=\operatorname{Pctl}_{p_{1j}}(\{X_{1t}\}).
\tag{5.10}\]
\[
B_{2k,t}=\operatorname{Pctl}_{p_{2k}}(\{X_{2t}\}).
\tag{5.11}\]
I use the 30th and 70th percentiles for beta and the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles for market capitalization.
Use the same percentile and membership functions as in the univariate sort. The second set of breakpoints is grouped only by year here. The dependent sort uses the same pipeline with an additional grouping key for the first portfolio.

control_ports = ["1", "2", "3"]

def bivariate_sort(first, second, *, dependent=False):
    stocks = annual_panel.filter(pl.all_horizontal(pl.col(first, second).is_finite()))
    first_breaks = breakpoints(stocks, first, [.30, .70], ["year"])
    first_groups = form_portfolios(stocks, first, first_breaks, ["year"], "control")

    by = ["year", "control"] if dependent else ["year"]
    breakpoint_sample = first_groups if dependent else stocks
    second_breaks = breakpoints(breakpoint_sample, second, [.25, .50, .75], by)
    members = form_portfolios(first_groups, second, second_breaks, by, "target")
    return members, first_breaks, second_breaks

independent, first_breaks, second_breaks = bivariate_sort("Beta", "MktCap")

5.2.3 Average Portfolio Values
Within each of the 12 portfolios, compute the outcome using the univariate weighting rule. The example uses equal weights.
\[
Y_{j,k,t}=\frac{\sum_{i\in P_{j,k,t}}W_{i,t}Y_{i,t}}
                {\sum_{i\in P_{j,k,t}}W_{i,t}}.
\tag{5.13}\]
A high-minus-low spread along market capitalization holds the beta group fixed. A spread along beta holds the market-cap group fixed.
\[
Y_{j,\mathrm{Diff},t}=Y_{j,n_2,t}-Y_{j,1,t}.
\tag{5.14}\]
\[
Y_{\mathrm{Diff},k,t}=Y_{n_1,k,t}-Y_{1,k,t}.
\tag{5.15}\]
The results can also be averaged across either set of portfolios. Each group receives equal weight, even when stock counts differ.
\[
Y_{\mathrm{Avg},k,t}=\frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_1}Y_{j,k,t}.
\tag{5.16}\]
\[
Y_{j,\mathrm{Avg},t}=\frac{1}{n_2}\sum_{k=1}^{n_2}Y_{j,k,t}.
\tag{5.17}\]
\[
Y_{\mathrm{Avg},\mathrm{Avg},t}
=\frac{1}{n_1}\sum_jY_{j,\mathrm{Avg},t}
=\frac{1}{n_2}\sum_kY_{\mathrm{Avg},k,t}
=\frac{1}{n_1n_2}\sum_j\sum_kY_{j,k,t}.
\tag{5.18}\]
The difference in differences compares the market-cap spread in the highest-beta group with the spread in the lowest-beta group. The same result comes from comparing beta spreads across market-cap groups.
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y_{\mathrm{Diff},\mathrm{Diff},t}
&=Y_{n_1,n_2,t}-Y_{n_1,1,t}-Y_{1,n_2,t}+Y_{1,1,t}\\
&=Y_{\mathrm{Diff},n_2,t}-Y_{\mathrm{Diff},1,t}\\
&=Y_{n_1,\mathrm{Diff},t}-Y_{1,\mathrm{Diff},t}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.19}\]

def bivariate_returns(members, *, dependent=False):
    cells = (
        members.filter(pl.col("year") < last_holding_year)
        .group_by("year", "control", "target").agg(pl.col("excess").mean())
    )
    grid = control_grid(cells, "excess")
    control_returns = pl.col(control_ports)
    spread = grid.group_by("year").agg(
        control_returns.filter(pl.col("target") == 4).first()
        - control_returns.filter(pl.col("target") == 1).first()
    ).with_columns(target=pl.lit(5))

    rows = [grid, spread.select(grid.columns)]
    if not dependent:
        average = grid.group_by("year").agg(pl.col(control_ports).mean()).with_columns(target=pl.lit(6))
        rows.append(average.select(grid.columns))
    return (
        pl.concat(rows).sort("year", "target")
        .with_columns(Diff=pl.col("3") - pl.col("1"),
                      Avg=pl.mean_horizontal(control_ports, ignore_nulls=False))
    )

P_{j,k,t}=

Conditional quartiles tend to distribute stocks evenly within each beta group. In the independent sort, the largest stocks are much more common in the high-beta group than in the low-beta group. Figure 5.2 compares average stock counts across the two sorts.


Code
sort_methods = ["Independent", "Dependent"]
average_counts = pl.concat(
    counts.group_by("control", "target").agg(count=pl.col("len").mean())
    .with_columns(method=pl.lit(method, dtype=pl.Enum(sort_methods)))
    for method, counts in zip(sort_methods, [independent_counts, dependent_counts], strict=True)
)
max_count = average_counts["count"].max()
(
    average_counts.with_columns(
        label=pl.col("count").round().cast(pl.Int64),
        label_color=pl.when(pl.col("count") > 0.58 * max_count)
        .then(pl.lit("white")).otherwise(pl.lit("#172b4d")),
    )
    .ggplot(aes(x="control", y="target", fill="count"))
    .geom_tile()
    .geom_text(aes(label="label", color="label_color"))
    .facet_wrap("method", nrow=1)
    .scale_fill_gradient(low="#f7fbff", high="#08306b", limits=(0, max_count), guide=None)
    .scale_color_identity()
    .scale_x_continuous(breaks=range(1, 4), expand=(0, 0))
    .scale_y_reverse(breaks=range(1, 5), expand=(0, 0))
    .labs(x="Beta group", y="Market-cap quartile")
    .theme_minimal()
    .add_theme(figure_size=(8, 4), panel_grid=element_blank())
)

title: 5  Portfolio Analysis
text:
5.4 Independent Versus Dependent Sort
Average market capitalization makes the difference between the two methods concrete. An independent sort applies the same market-cap cutoffs across beta groups. A dependent sort can classify a stock as large among low-beta stocks even if its capitalization would place it in a lower quartile among high-beta stocks.

def average_capitalization(members):
    return (
        members.group_by("year", "control", "target").agg(pl.col("MktCap").mean())
        .group_by("control", "target").agg(pl.col("MktCap").mean())
        .pivot(on="control", index="target", values="MktCap")
        .sort("target").select("target", *control_ports)
    )

independent_caps = average_capitalization(independent)
dependent_caps = average_capitalization(dependent)

title: 6  Fama and Macbeth Regression Analysis
text:
6.1 Implementation
This chapter uses BEM’s methodologies sample from Chapter 2 to illustrate the two steps of a Fama–MacBeth regression. The first step fits a cross-sectional regression in each formation year. The second averages the coefficients across years and estimates their standard errors from the time series of annual coefficients.

6.2 Interpreting FM Regressions
The ordinary Fama–MacBeth standard error is the standard deviation of the annual slopes divided by the square root of the number of years. For the size slope in the regression with all three characteristics, compare the ordinary \(t\)-statistic with the six-lag Newey–West \(t\)-statistic.

    "t": [size_slopes.mean() / ordinary_se, fits[-1].tvalues["Size"]],

title: 7  The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
text:
7.1 The US Stock Market
This chapter reconstructs the figures and tables in Chapter 7 of Bali et al. (2016). I use a later snapshot of legacy CRSP (SIZ), the same data format used by the authors. See Table 1.1 for source update dates.
crumbs: Part II. The Cross Section of Stock Returns
7  The CRSP Sample and Market Factor

title: 7  The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
text:
7.1.1 The CRSP US-Based Common Stock Sample
At each calendar month-end, keep securities with a historical share code of 10 or 11. I do not restrict the exchange or require a price to count a stock. For market capitalization, use the absolute alternate price times shares outstanding. Dividing by 1,000 gives millions of dollars because CRSP reports shares in thousands.

import polars as pl

from eap_pl import load_parquet

first = pl.date(1925, 12, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 12, 1)

msf = (
    load_parquet("msf", "crsp")
    .with_columns(month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start())
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first, last))
    .select(
        "permno", "month", "date", "altprc", "prc", "ret",
        cap=pl.when((pl.col("altprc") != 0) & (pl.col("shrout") > 0))
        .then((pl.col("altprc") * pl.col("shrout")).abs() / 1000),
    )
)

names = (
    load_parquet("msenames", "crsp")
    .filter(
        pl.col("shrcd").is_in([10, 11]),
        pl.col("namedt") <= last.dt.month_end(),
        pl.col("nameendt") >= first,
    )
    .with_columns(
        month=pl.date_ranges(
            pl.max_horizontal(pl.col("namedt").dt.month_start(), first),
            pl.min_horizontal(pl.col("nameendt").dt.month_start(), last),
            interval="1mo",
        )
    )
    .explode("month")
    .filter(pl.col("month").dt.month_end().is_between("namedt", "nameendt"))
    .select("permno", "month", "exchcd", "siccd")
)
universe = names.join(msf, on=["permno", "month"], how="left", validate="1:1")

factors = (
    load_parquet("factors_monthly", "ff")
    .select(pl.col("date").dt.month_start().alias("month"), "mktrf", "rf")
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first, last))
)

cpi = (
    pl.read_csv("data/cpi-aucns.csv", try_parse_dates=True)
    .rename({"observation_date": "month", "CPIAUCNS": "cpi"})
)
if cpi.filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first, last))["month"].n_unique() != 1045:
    raise ValueError("Refresh the CPI file for December 1925–December 2012; see README.")
cpi_2012 = cpi.filter(pl.col("month") == last)["cpi"].item()



7.1.2 Composition of the CRSP Sample
Figures 7.1–7.4 of Bali et al. (2016) decompose the sample by exchange and industry from December 1925 to December 2012. Count every stock in the month-end universe, even if market capitalization is missing. For market value, sum only observed capitalization. Convert nominal millions to billions of December 2012 dollars using the ratio of December 2012 CPI to that month’s CPI.

Stock Exchange Composition of CRSP Sample
The book groups exchange codes 1 and 31 as NYSE, 2 and 32 as AMEX, and 3 and 33 as Nasdaq. All remaining codes go into Other.

from plotnine_polars import aes, guide_legend

exchange = (
    pl.when(pl.col("exchcd").is_in([1, 31])).then(pl.lit("NYSE"))
    .when(pl.col("exchcd").is_in([2, 32])).then(pl.lit("AMEX"))
    .when(pl.col("exchcd").is_in([3, 33])).then(pl.lit("Nasdaq"))
    .otherwise(pl.lit("Other"))
)

composition = (
    universe
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(pl.date(1925, 12, 1), pl.date(2012, 12, 1)))
    .select("month", "cap", "siccd", exchange=exchange)
    .join(cpi.lazy(), on="month", how="left", validate="m:1")
    .with_columns(real_cap=pl.col("cap") * cpi_2012 / pl.col("cpi") / 1000)
    .collect()
)

assert composition["cpi"].is_not_null().all()
assert composition["cpi"].gt(0).all()
assert composition["month"].n_unique() == 1045

def summarize_composition(sample, group, labels):
    summary = sample.group_by("month", group).agg(
        stocks=pl.len(),
        value=pl.col("real_cap").sum(),
    )
    grid = sample.select("month").unique().join(
        pl.DataFrame({group: labels}), how="cross"
    )
    return (
        grid
        .join(summary, on=["month", group], how="left", validate="1:1")
        .with_columns(pl.col("stocks", "value").fill_null(0))
        .sort("month")
    )

exchange_labels = ["NYSE", "AMEX", "Nasdaq", "Other"]
by_exchange = summarize_composition(composition, "exchange", exchange_labels)
total = (
    by_exchange
    .group_by("month")
    .agg(pl.col("stocks", "value").sum())
    .with_columns(exchange=pl.lit("Total"))
    .select(by_exchange.columns)
)
by_exchange = pl.concat([total, by_exchange])

def plot_composition(data, group, labels, measure, y_label):
    colors = [
        "#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e", "#2ca02c", "#d62728", "#9467bd", "#8c564b",
        "#e377c2", "#7f7f7f", "#bcbd22", "#17becf", "#aec7e8", "#ffbb78",
    ]
    palette = dict(zip(labels, colors))
    if "Total" in palette:
        palette["Total"] = "black"
    return (
        data.ggplot(aes(x="month", y=measure, color=group))
        .geom_line()
        .scale_x_date(date_breaks="10 years", date_labels="%Y")
        .scale_y_continuous(limits=(0, None), expand=(0, 0, 0.05, 0))
        .scale_color_manual(values=palette, breaks=labels, guide=guide_legend(ncol=3))
        .labs(x="Month", y=y_label, color="")
        .theme_minimal()
        .add_theme(figure_size=(9, 4.5), legend_position="bottom")
    )



Code
plot_composition(by_exchange, "exchange", ["Total", *exchange_labels],
                 "stocks", "Number of stocks")








Figure 7.1: Number of stocks by exchange, recreating the series in BEM Figure 7.1.







Code
plot_composition(by_exchange, "exchange", ["Total", *exchange_labels],
                 "value", "Market value ($ billions, December 2012)")








Figure 7.2: Market value by exchange, recreating the series in BEM Figure 7.2.





AMEX enters the data in July 1962. Most Nasdaq coverage starts in December 1972. The value series jumps much less than the count series at those dates: market coverage can change substantially without much change in market value. Keep that distinction in mind when comparing equal- and value-weighted results across time.
The December 2012 stock count includes 86 stocks in the Other category, of which 85 have no usable capitalization.1


Industry Composition of CRSP Sample
I use the security’s current SIC code rather than a code carried back from a later date. OSHA’s SIC manual describes the divisions. The table uses the intervals in BEM Table 7.1, with shortened labels. Keep zero and null codes separate from nonmissing codes that do not fall in a listed interval.

title: 7  The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
text:
7.2 Stock Returns and Excess Returns
Start with eligible common stocks at the end of month \(t\) and look up the return for the same security in month \(t+1\). Do not require it to remain in the common-stock universe in the holding month: that would screen out delistings.
Chapter 7 uses the legacy CRSP delisting return in place of the regular monthly return if the stock delists. If no delisting return is recorded, it imputes a loss of 30% for the codes listed below and a loss of 100% for other delistings. This is the book’s convention for legacy data, not a reason to adjust the reported returns from CRSP CIZ a second time.

first_return = pl.date(1926, 7, 1)
first_return_late = pl.date(1963, 7, 1)
hold_month = pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo")

delist = (
    load_parquet("msedelist", "crsp")
    .with_columns(month=pl.col("dlstdt").dt.month_start())
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first_return, last))
    .select("permno", "month", "dlret", "dlstcd")
)
poor_performance = (
    pl.col("dlstcd").is_in([500, 520, 580, 584])
    | pl.col("dlstcd").is_between(551, 574)
)
imputed_delist = pl.when(poor_performance).then(-0.30).otherwise(-1.00)

return_panel = (
    universe
    .with_columns(formation_month="month")
    .with_columns(month=hold_month)
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first_return, last))
    .drop("ret")
    .join(
        msf.select("permno", "month", ret_raw="ret"),
        on=["permno", "month"], how="left", validate="1:1",
    )
    .join(delist, on=["permno", "month"], how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(factors.select("month", "rf"), on="month", how="left", validate="m:1")
    .with_columns(
        ret_adj=pl.when(pl.col("dlstcd").is_not_null())
        .then(pl.coalesce("dlret", imputed_delist))
        .otherwise(pl.col("ret_raw"))
    )
    .with_columns(
        excess_raw=pl.col("ret_raw") - pl.col("rf"),
        excess_adj=pl.col("ret_adj") - pl.col("rf"),
    )
)

The Fama–French risk-free return applies to the holding month, not the formation month. I first calculate the statistics across stocks for each return month, then average those monthly statistics. In particular, the means give each month equal weight, irrespective of the number of stocks in that month. I use sample standard deviations, bias-adjusted skewness and excess kurtosis, and linearly interpolated quantiles.

def summarize_returns(start):
    x = pl.col("return_pct")
    return (
        return_panel
        .filter(pl.col("month") >= start)
        .select("month", "excess_adj", "ret_adj", "excess_raw", "ret_raw")
        .unpivot(index="month", variable_name="series", value_name="return_pct")
        .with_columns(return_pct=100 * x)
        .group_by("month", "series")
        .agg(
            n=x.count(),
            mean=x.mean(),
            sd=x.std(),
            skew=x.skew(bias=False),
            excess_kurtosis=x.kurtosis(fisher=True, bias=False),
            min=x.min(),
            p05=x.quantile(0.05, interpolation="linear"),
            p25=x.quantile(0.25, interpolation="linear"),
            median=x.median(),
            p75=x.quantile(0.75, interpolation="linear"),
            p95=x.quantile(0.95, interpolation="linear"),
            max=x.max(),
        )
        .group_by("series")
        .agg(pl.exclude("month", "series").mean())
        .collect()
    )

def display_returns(table):
    labels = {
        "excess_adj": "Adjusted excess",
        "ret_adj": "Adjusted total",
        "excess_raw": "Unadjusted excess",
        "ret_raw": "Unadjusted total",
    }
    return (
        table
        .with_columns(series=pl.col("series").replace_strict(labels))
        .unpivot(index="series", variable_name="statistic", value_name="value")
        .pivot(on="series", index="statistic", values="value")
        .select("statistic", *labels.values())
        .with_columns(pl.exclude("statistic").round(2))
    )

table_7_3 = summarize_returns(first_return_late)

title: 7  The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
text:
7.3 The Market Factor
The Fama–French market factor (mkt) is the excess return on a broad value-weighted portfolio of US common stocks. CRSP’s value-weighted market index (vwretd) has a broader set of eligible securities. I put both measures on an excess-return basis by subtracting the risk-free rate (rf) from vwretd. mkt already has the risk-free rate subtracted.

market = (
    factors
    .rename({"mktrf": "mkt"})
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(pl.date(1926, 7, 1), pl.date(2012, 12, 1)))
    .join(
        load_parquet("msi", "crsp")
        .select(month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start(), vwretd=pl.col("vwretd")),
        on="month", how="left", validate="1:1",
    )
    .with_columns(
        vw_excess=pl.col("vwretd") - pl.col("rf"),
        log_excess=pl.col("mkt").log1p(),
    )
    .sort("month")
    .collect()
)

The monthly correlation between mkt and the adjusted CRSP return (vw_excess) is 0.9995 in this data vintage. Following Bali et al. (2016, sec. 7.3), I summarize the monthly returns from July 1926 through December 2012. The annualized Sharpe ratio uses \(\sqrt{12}\) times the ratio of the monthly mean to the monthly standard deviation, as in the book.


Code
import eap_pl

series_labels = {
    "mkt": "`mkt`",
    "vw_excess": "`vwretd` less `rf`",
    "log_excess": "Log `mkt`",
}
returns = pl.col(*series_labels)
market_summary = (
    market.select(
        pl.lit(list(series_labels.values())).alias("Series"),
        pl.concat_list(returns.mean() * 100).alias("Monthly mean (%)"),
        pl.concat_list(returns.std() * 100).alias("Monthly SD (%)"),
        pl.concat_list(returns.mean() * 12**0.5 / returns.std())
        .alias("Annualized Sharpe"),
    )
    .explode(pl.all())
    .with_columns(pl.col(pl.Float64).round(3))
)
market_summary.with_columns(pl.col(pl.Float64).cast(pl.String)).eap.show_table()

Cumulative market excess returns
For comparison with BEM Figure 7.5, I compound the monthly market factor, \(\prod_{s\leq t}(1+\mathrm{MKT}_s)-1\), and sum its log transformation, \(\sum_{s\leq t}\log(1+\mathrm{MKT}_s)\). Both are transformations of the same underlying series. The panels share a month-end date axis and use separate percentage scales.
Compounding the market factor is not the same as subtracting the compounded risk-free return from the compounded market return. Here I follow the book’s definition.

market_path = market.with_columns(
    date=pl.col("month").dt.month_end(),
    compounded=(1 + pl.col("mkt")).cum_prod() - 1,
    cumulative_log=pl.col("log_excess").cum_sum(),
)

Drawdowns
The compounded line makes early losses look small compared with later ones. To measure a drawdown, divide the value at the trough by the value at the preceding peak, then subtract one. Use the peak and trough months described in BEM; the recovery month is the first later month back at or above the old peak. Month names here refer to end-of-month values, so an episode that begins in September uses the August close as its reference.


Code
from datetime import date

episodes = [
    ("1929 crash", date(1929, 8, 1), date(1932, 6, 1)),
    ("1968–1974 decline", date(1968, 11, 1), date(1974, 9, 1)),
    ("Dot-com bust and financial crisis", date(2000, 3, 1), date(2009, 2, 1)),
    ("1987 crash", date(1987, 8, 1), date(1987, 11, 1)),
]

wealth = market_path.select("month", wealth=1 + pl.col("compounded"))

def measure_drawdown(episode, peak, trough):
    peak_value = wealth.filter(pl.col("month") == peak)["wealth"].item()
    trough_value = wealth.filter(pl.col("month") == trough)["wealth"].item()
    recovery = wealth.filter(
        (pl.col("month") > trough) & (pl.col("wealth") >= peak_value)
    )["month"].first()
    return {
        "Episode": episode,
        "Peak": peak.strftime("%Y-%m"),
        "Trough": trough.strftime("%Y-%m"),
        "Drawdown (%)": round(100 * (trough_value / peak_value - 1), 1),
        "Recovery": recovery.strftime("%Y-%m") if recovery else "Not by 2012-12",
    }

pl.DataFrame([measure_drawdown(*episode) for episode in episodes])

title: 7  The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
text:
7.4 The CAPM Risk Model
BEM §7.4 introduces the specification rather than reporting another empirical table. To adjust a portfolio for its market exposure, regress its excess return \(r_{p,t}\) on the market excess return:
\[
r_{p,t} = \alpha_p + \beta_p\mathrm{MKT}_t + \varepsilon_{p,t}.
\]
The intercept \(\alpha_p\) is the average monthly abnormal return under this model; \(\beta_p\) is the sensitivity to the market. A portfolio long one group and short another is already a difference in returns, so subtracting the risk-free rate from both legs cancels out. Chapter 9 applies this logic and also considers the Fama–French three-factor model.

title: 8  Beta
text:
8.1 Estimating Beta
I reconstruct Tables 8.1–8.6 of Bali et al. (2016). The sample consists of CRSP common stocks at the end of each month from June 1963 through November 2012. I use legacy CRSP daily and monthly stock returns and the corresponding Fama–French factors. See Table 1.1 for the source vintages.
The CAPM predicts that a stock’s expected excess return is its market beta times the market risk premium, \(\mathbb E[r_i]=\beta_i\mathbb E[MKT]\). To estimate beta, regress the stock’s historical excess return \(r_{i,s}=R_{i,s}-R_{f,s}\) on the market excess return \(MKT_s\), with an intercept. For stock \(i\) at the end of month \(t\),
\[
r_{i,s}=\alpha_i+\beta_i MKT_s+\varepsilon_{i,s},
\qquad
\widehat\beta_{i,t}
=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}_{s\in W_t}(r_{i,s},MKT_s)}
{\operatorname{Var}_{s\in W_t}(MKT_s)},
\]
where \(W_t\) is the estimation window ending in month \(t\). Both moments use the same dates with valid stock and market returns. BEM use the following windows and minimum observation counts (§8.1).
Suppose a stock trades infrequently. Its return may reflect news that first moved the market on a different trading day. BEM consider two adjustments that use a year of daily returns and a 200-observation minimum. Scholes–Williams uses three separate slopes \(b_{-1}\), \(b_0\), and \(b_{+1}\) from regressing \(r_{i,s}\) on \(MKT_{s+k}\) one at a time. Dimson uses the slopes \(\gamma_k\) from one regression with all eleven market returns from \(s-5\) through \(s+5\) as predictors.
\[
\widehat\beta^{SW}_{i,t}
=\frac{\widehat b_{-1}+\widehat b_0+\widehat b_{+1}}{1+2\widehat\rho_M},
\qquad
\widehat\beta^{D}_{i,t}=\sum_{k=-5}^{5}\widehat\gamma_k,
\]
where \(\widehat\rho_M\) is the market return’s first-order autocorrelation over the estimation window. I shift the market series on the trading calendar before joining it to stock returns. A lag can precede the first stock-return date in the window. I omit response dates whose market lead falls after formation and apply the minimum to the remaining complete observations. This keeps all beta inputs observable at formation.
import polars as pl

from eap_pl import load_beta_universe, load_daily_beta_inputs, load_parquet

first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)
last_holding = last.dt.offset_by("1mo")
keys = ["permno", "month"]

universe = load_beta_universe(first, last).collect()
I screen for common shares at formation using historical share codes 10 and 11. A stock can contribute its earlier returns to the estimation window even if its historical share code changed. I use CRSP’s reported returns for estimation and apply the delisting convention in Section 7.2 to the next-month returns used to evaluate the beta estimates.
monthly_stock = (
    load_parquet("msf", "crsp")
    .filter(pl.col("date").is_between(
        first.dt.offset_by("-59mo"), last_holding.dt.month_end()
    ))
    .select(
        "permno",
        month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start(),
        ret=pl.col("ret").cast(pl.Float64),
        cap=pl.when((pl.col("altprc") != 0) & (pl.col("shrout") > 0))
        .then(pl.col("altprc").abs() * pl.col("shrout")),
    )
)
monthly_market = load_parquet("factors_monthly", "ff").select(
    pl.col("date").dt.month_start().alias("month"), "mktrf", "rf",
)
monthly_excess = (
    monthly_stock.join(monthly_market, on="month", validate="m:1")
    .select(*keys, "mktrf", retrf=pl.col("ret") - pl.col("rf"))
    .filter(pl.all_horizontal(pl.col("retrf", "mktrf").is_finite()))
)

def beta_slope(stock, market):
    return pl.cov(stock, market) / pl.col(market).var()
The covariance-over-variance formula applies directly to monthly returns. I include the formation dates in the rolling index so a window is evaluated even if the current month’s return is missing. The window is open at its left endpoint and includes the formation month.
monthly_windows = {"1Y": (12, 10), "2Y": (24, 20), "3Y": (36, 24), "5Y": (60, 24)}
daily_windows = {"1M": (1, 15), "3M": (3, 50), "6M": (6, 100),
                 "12M": (12, 200), "24M": (24, 450)}

monthly_returns = (
    universe.lazy()
    .join(monthly_excess, on=keys, how="full", coalesce=True, validate="1:1")
    .sort(keys)
    .collect()
)

def monthly_beta(label, months, minimum):
    return (
        monthly_returns
        .rolling("month", period=f"{months}mo", group_by="permno")
        .agg(
            beta_slope("retrf", "mktrf").alias(label),
            pl.col("retrf").count().alias("n"),
        )
        .select(
            *keys,
            pl.when((pl.col("n") >= minimum) & pl.col(label).is_finite())
            .then(pl.col(label)),
        )
    )
For daily returns, each trading day enters many windows. I sum the regression inputs once per stock and month, then roll those sums across months. For example, the slope uses \(\sum xy-(\sum x)(\sum y)/n\) divided by \(\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2/n\). The adjusted regressions use the same idea with cross-products between market returns at different offsets.
daily_factors, daily_excess = load_daily_beta_inputs(
    first.dt.offset_by("-23mo"), last.dt.month_end(),
)
The tables in this chapter end with November 2012 formation, followed by December 2012 holding returns. Several later chapters also use the 12-month daily beta. I could save those estimates to a Parquet file for reuse across chapters. On my machine, eap_pl.load_monthly_betas() takes about 1.2 seconds to calculate this beta for the full sample, so I calculate it on demand.

title: 8  Beta
text:
8.2 Summary Statistics
Table 8.1 averages monthly cross-sectional statistics. The count is the average number of stocks with an available estimate in a month. For example, the dispersion of the one-month daily beta reflects both differences in stocks’ exposures and estimation noise from short return histories. I use sample standard deviations, bias-adjusted skewness and excess kurtosis, and linearly interpolated quantiles.

beta_long = betas.unpivot(
    on=beta_labels, index=keys, variable_name="measure", value_name="beta",
)
b = pl.col("beta")
summary = (
    beta_long.group_by("measure", "month")
    .agg(
        mean=b.mean(), sd=b.std(), skew=b.skew(bias=False),
        kurt=b.kurtosis(fisher=True, bias=False), min=b.min(),
        p05=b.quantile(.05, interpolation="linear"),
        p25=b.quantile(.25, interpolation="linear"), median=b.median(),
        p75=b.quantile(.75, interpolation="linear"),
        p95=b.quantile(.95, interpolation="linear"), max=b.max(), n=b.count(),

    .group_by("measure")

8.3 Correlations
Table 8.2 reports the mean of the monthly correlations. For each pair, I use stocks for which both estimates are available. Winsorize each beta within month at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles for Pearson correlations below the diagonal. Use the original values for Spearman rank correlations above the diagonal.

    pl.col(beta_labels).eap.winsorize(prob=0.005, quantile_method="linear").over("month")
)

def mean_correlations(panel, method):
    return (
        panel.group_by("month")
        .agg(
            pl.corr(a, b, method=method).alias(f"{a}:{b}")
            for i, a in enumerate(beta_labels) for b in beta_labels[i + 1:]
        )
        .select(pl.exclude("month").fill_nan(None).mean())
        .row(0, named=True)
    )

spearman = mean_correlations(betas, "spearman")

title: 8  Beta
text:
8.4 Persistence
Table 8.3 compares a stock’s winsorized beta with its beta exactly \(\tau\) calendar months later. I calculate a Pearson correlation across stocks in each month and average over months. I leave cells blank when the stock-return windows overlap. This helps distinguish persistence from the effect of using some of the same returns twice.

def persistence(lag):
    columns = [b for b in beta_labels if window_months[b] <= lag]
    current = clipped.select(*keys, *columns)
    future = current.with_columns(month=pl.col("month").dt.offset_by(f"-{lag}mo"))
    return (
        current.join(future, on=keys, suffix="_future", validate="1:1")
        .group_by("month")
        .agg(pl.corr(b, f"{b}_future").alias(b) for b in columns)
        .select(pl.lit(lag).alias("Lag (months)"), pl.col(columns).fill_nan(None).mean())
    )

persistence_table = pl.concat(
    [persistence(lag) for lag in [1, 3, 6, 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 120]],
    how="diagonal",
)

title: 9  The Size Effect
text:
9.1 Calculating Market Capitalization
I follow Chapter 9 of Bali et al. (2016). I compare monthly and June-based size, then examine how each relates to subsequent stock returns. Formation months run from June 1963 through November 2012.
The book was published in 2016, well before CRSP’s CIZ format. This replication uses the legacy (SIZ) monthly stock and names files, not the CIZ files used in the earlier chapters. I use a newer legacy snapshot than the authors, with the same sample dates. See Table 1.1 for the embedded update dates.
Use the share code in force at the end of each month. Keep share codes 10 and 11, without adding an exchange screen. The book’s measure uses the absolute alternate price and shares outstanding. CRSP records shares in thousands; dividing their product by 1,000 gives market capitalization in millions of dollars. Treat zeros as missing.
For the annual measure, join each stock to its capitalization at the most recent June. A stock without a record for that particular June has no annual value. I do not carry forward an older June observation.
Convert nominal market capitalization to December 2012 dollars using the BLS CPI-U, not seasonally adjusted. Use the CPI for the current observation month for both the monthly and the June-based measures, as in the book.
import polars as pl

from eap_pl import build_sizes

first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)
all_sizes = build_sizes()
sizes = all_sizes.filter(
    pl.col("common"), pl.col("month").is_between(first, last),
)
The table includes the earlier December market equity needed for book-to-market and December 2012 for the methodologies sample. It records common-stock eligibility separately so the prior December price remains available when a stock’s share code changes.

    load_parquet("msenames", "crsp")

title: 10  The Value Premium
text:
10.1 Calculating Book-to-Market Ratio
I follow Chapter 10 of Bali et al. (2016). Book-to-market compares an accounting measure of equity with what investors pay for the shares. I ask how this ratio varies across stocks and whether it predicts the following month’s excess return.
BEM calculate the book value of common equity from Compustat’s North America Fundamentals Annual file (comp.funda) (2016, sec. 10.1). They start with stockholders’ equity (seq), add deferred taxes (txdb) and the investment tax credit (itcb), and subtract the book value of preferred stock. All amounts are in millions of dollars.
For preferred stock, BEM use redemption value (pstkrv) if available, then liquidation value (pstkl), then par value (pstk). They use zero if all three preferred stock fields are missing, and likewise set a missing investment tax credit to zero. Book equity is missing if either seq or txdb is missing.
BEM use industrial-format records (indfmt = "INDL") with standard data format (datafmt = "STD"). If a firm reports more than one fiscal year-end in a calendar year, I follow BEM in taking the record with the latest fiscal year-end (datadate).
Use CRSP–Compustat links valid on the fiscal year-end. When a direct link is unavailable, try an unambiguous historical CUSIP match. I use the legacy monthly names file for this fallback.
Divide book equity by the nominal December capitalization for the same calendar year, from Chapter 9. Make that ratio available at the end of the following June and carry it through the next May. This gives a December fiscal year-end at least six months before the ratio enters a portfolio sort.
import polars as pl

from eap_pl import build_book_to_market, build_sizes

first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)
keys = ["permno", "month"]

all_sizes = build_sizes()
book_to_market = build_book_to_market(all_sizes)
For this chapter, use positive book equity so the logarithm is defined. The table also keeps the signed ratio for the annual summaries in Section 2.2.

    load_parquet("funda", "comp")

    .select(
        "gvkey", "datadate", year=pl.col("datadate").dt.year(),
        cusip=pl.col("cusip").str.slice(0, 8),

        - pl.coalesce("pstkrv", "pstkl", "pstk", pl.lit(0)),

    .filter(pl.col("datadate") == pl.col("datadate").max().over("gvkey", "year"))

    load_parquet("ccmxpf_lnkused", "crsp")
    .filter(pl.col("usedflag") == 1, pl.col("ulinktype").is_in(["LU", "LC"]), pl.col("upermno") > 0)

    funda.join(links, on="gvkey")
    .filter(pl.col("datadate") >= pl.col("start"),
            (pl.col("datadate") <= pl.col("end")) | pl.col("end").is_null())
    .select("gvkey", *annual_keys, "be").unique()
)
cusips = load_parquet("msenames", "crsp").select("permno", "namedt", "nameendt", cusip="ncusip")
cusip_book = (
    funda.join(linked_book.select("gvkey", "year"), on=["gvkey", "year"], how="anti")
    .filter(pl.col("cusip").str.len_chars() == 8)
    .join(cusips, on="cusip")
    .filter(pl.col("datadate").is_between("namedt", "nameendt"))
    .select("gvkey", *annual_keys, "be").unique()
    .filter(pl.len().over("gvkey", "year") == 1)
)
book = (
    pl.concat([linked_book, cusip_book])
    .filter(pl.len().over(*annual_keys) == 1, pl.col("be").is_finite())
    .select(*annual_keys, "be")
)

december_cap = (
    sizes.lazy().filter(pl.col("month").dt.month() == 12)
    .select("permno", year=pl.col("month").dt.year(), me="cap")
)
book_to_market = (
    book.join(december_cap, on=["permno", "year"], validate="1:1")
    .with_columns(
        available=pl.date(pl.col("year") + 1, 6, 1),
        bm_raw=pl.col("be") / pl.col("me"),
    )
    .with_columns(
        month=pl.date_ranges(
            pl.col("available"), pl.col("available").dt.offset_by("11mo"),
            interval="1mo",
        ),
        bm=pl.when(pl.col("bm_raw") > 0).then(pl.col("bm_raw")),
    )
    .explode("month")
    .filter(pl.col("month") <= last.dt.offset_by("1mo"))
    .select(*keys, book_year="year", be="be", me="me", bm_raw="bm_raw",
            bm="bm", log_bm=pl.col("bm").log())
    .collect()
)

title: 10  The Value Premium
text:
10.2 Summary Statistics
The numerator and denominator come from the same annual vintage. For the dollar amounts in the table, express both in December 2012 dollars using the CPI for the observation month. The common deflator leaves the book-to-market ratio unchanged.

from eap_pl import mean_cross_sections, monthly_panel

panel = monthly_panel(sizes, first, last).join(book_to_market, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
cpi = pl.read_csv("data/cpi-aucns.csv", try_parse_dates=True).rename(
    {"observation_date": "month", "CPIAUCNS": "cpi"}
)
cpi_2012 = cpi.filter(pl.col("month") == pl.date(2012, 12, 1))["cpi"].item()
value_panel = (
    panel.filter(pl.col("bm").is_not_null())
    .join(cpi, on="month", validate="m:1")
    .with_columns(
        be_real=pl.col("be") * cpi_2012 / pl.col("cpi"),
        me_real=pl.col("me") * cpi_2012 / pl.col("cpi"),
    )
)

10.5 Book-to-Market Ratio and Stock Returns

10.5.1 Univariate Portfolio Analysis
Form ten portfolios at the end of each month using the book-to-market ratio. Compare breakpoints from all eligible stocks with breakpoints from NYSE stocks. 10.5.2 Bivariate Portfolio Analysis
Sort first on a control variable, then on book-to-market within each control quintile. This asks whether the return difference between high and low book-to-market stocks persists among stocks of similar beta or size.


Code
average_portfolios, differences = [], []
for control, label in [("beta", "Beta"), ("cap", "Market cap")]:
    portfolios = bivariate_months(panel, control, "bm", nyse=False, dependent=True)
    for weight in ("EW", "VW"):
        averages, spreads = bivariate_panel(portfolios, weight, independent=False, spread_only=True)
        average_portfolios.append(averages.rename({"Target": "Portfolio"}).with_columns(
            pl.lit("Across control quintiles").alias("Panel"),
            pl.lit(label).alias("Sort"), pl.lit(weight).alias("Weights"),
        ))
        differences.append(spreads.rename({
            "Control": "Portfolio", "5–1 excess return": "Excess return", "5–1 CAPM alpha": "CAPM alpha",
        }).with_columns(
            pl.lit("`bm` 5–1 within control quintile").alias("Panel"),
            pl.lit(label).alias("Sort"), pl.lit(weight).alias("Weights"),
        ))
pl.concat(differences + average_portfolios).select(
    "Panel", "Sort", "Weights", "Portfolio", "Excess return", "CAPM alpha",
).eap.show_table()

        .with_columns(pl.lit(weight).alias("Weights"))

title: 10  The Value Premium
text:
10.6 The Value Factor
hml averages the high-book-to-market portfolios across the two size groups and subtracts the average of their low-book-to-market counterparts. Using small and big stocks on both sides reduces the weight of the size effect in the comparison. I use the published monthly Fama–French hml series from July 1926 through December 2012.


Code
from eap_pl import plot_factor

plot_factor("hml")








Figure 10.1: Cumulative returns on the Fama–French hml factor (BEM Figure 10.1)





In the Fama–French three-factor model, the intercept measures the portfolio’s return after accounting for exposures to market, size, and value factors. For excess portfolio return \(r_{p,t}\), the regression is
\[
r_{p,t}=\alpha_p+\beta_{p,M}MKT_t+\beta_{p,S}SMB_t+\beta_{p,H}HML_t+\varepsilon_{p,t}.
\]

title: 11  The Momentum Effect
text:
11.1 Measuring Momentum
Do stocks that recently outperformed continue to outperform? Following Chapter 11 of Bali et al. (2016), I compare seven measures of prior returns and examine how their predictive power changes with the return horizon. Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) document that portfolios buying recent winners and selling recent losers earn positive returns over several months.
At the end of month \(t\), the main measure compounds returns from \(t-11\) through \(t-1\). Skipping month \(t\) separates the signal from the most recent return, which is used to measure short-term reversal.
\[
\operatorname{Mom}_{i,t}
=100\left[\prod_{m=t-11}^{t-1}(1+R_{i,m})-1\right].
\tag{11.1}\]
In BEM’s Equation (11.1), \(R_{i,m}\) is the stock’s monthly return in decimal form and \(\operatorname{Mom}_{i,t}\) is measured in percentage points. I compound the available returns and require at least nine observations. For the lagged 12- and six-month alternatives, the minimum counts are ten and five. For the 12-, nine-, six-, and three-month windows that include month \(t\), the minimum counts are ten, seven, five, and three, respectively.
A calendar window counts months even when the CRSP file has a gap. The offset determines whether the window ends in month \(t\) or in month \(t-1\).
Count the nonmissing gross returns before taking their product.
import polars as pl

from eap_pl import build_book_to_market, build_momentum, build_sizes, monthly_panel

first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)
keys = ["permno", "month"]
signals = {
    "mom": "`mom`", "lag12": "Rₜ₋₁₂:ₜ₋₁", "lag6": "Rₜ₋₆:ₜ₋₁",
    "r12m": "`r12m`", "r9m": "`r9m`", "r6m": "`r6m`", "r3m": "`r3m`",
}

sizes = build_sizes()
book_to_market = build_book_to_market(sizes).select(*keys, "bm")
panel = (
    monthly_panel(sizes, first, last)
    .join(build_momentum(first, last), on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(book_to_market, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
)
The formation sample runs from June 1963 through November 2012. The panel uses the beta, size, and positive book-to-market measures from Chapter 8, Chapter 9, and Chapter 10. Holding-month excess returns use the delisting treatment in Section 7.2.

def _compound_trailing_return(returns, name, length, skip, minimum):
    gross = pl.col("gross")
    return returns.rolling(
        "month", period=f"{length}mo", offset=f"-{length + skip}mo",
        group_by="permno", closed="right",
    ).agg(
        pl.when(gross.count() >= minimum).then(100 * (gross.product() - 1)).alias(name)
    )
