text:
11.4 Momentum and Stock Returns

11.4.1 Univariate Portfolio Analysis
Each month, sort the stocks with a valid signal into ten portfolios using breakpoints from all stocks with that signal. Value weights use market capitalization at formation. Returns and alphas are in percentage points per month. For each winner-minus-loser spread, regress the monthly return series on an intercept, on the market factor, or on the three Fama–French factors to estimate its mean, CAPM alpha, or FF alpha. Parentheses report six-lag Newey–West \(t\)-statistics (Newey and West 1987).

from eap_pl import format_fit, hac, load_parquet
from eap_pl._portfolios import assign_portfolio, portfolio_months, spread

factors = (
    load_parquet("factors_monthly", "ff")
    .select(
        month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start(),
        market=100 * pl.col("mktrf"),
        smb=100 * pl.col("smb"),
        hml=100 * pl.col("hml"),
        rf=100 * pl.col("rf"),
    )
    .collect()
)
ff3 = ["market", "smb", "hml"]
weights = {"VW": "Value weighted", "EW": "Equal weighted"}


def spread_statistics(series, weight, *, ff_factors=ff3, capm=True):
    sample = (series.select("month", weight)
              .join(factors, on="month", validate="m:1").sort("month"))
    models = {"Return": "1"}
    if capm:
        models["CAPM α"] = "market"
    models["FF α"] = " + ".join(ff_factors)
    return {
        name: format_fit(hac(f"{weight} ~ {rhs}", sample), "Intercept")
        for name, rhs in models.items()
    }


deciles = {str(i): i for i in range(1, 11)}
formation = panel.select(*keys, "cap", *signals)
members = {
    signal: assign_portfolio(
        formation.select(*keys, "cap", signal).filter(pl.col(signal).is_finite()),
        signal, 10, "month",
    ).drop(signal)
    for signal in signals
}

one_month = panel.select(*keys, "market", "excess")
decile_returns = {
    signal: portfolio_months(
        stocks.join(one_month, on=keys, validate="1:1")
        .with_columns(pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo")),
        ["portfolio"],
    )
    for signal, stocks in members.items()
}

11.4.2 Returns at Longer Horizons
Keep the formation-month decile assignments and capitalization weights. For each \(k\), attach the return in month \(t+k\) and compute the spread across stocks with a return in that month. A delisting contributes its adjusted return in the month it occurs. I use realized returns through December 2012 and match the factors to the month in which each return is realized.

from eap_pl._data import monthly_stock_returns

holding_returns = (
    monthly_stock_returns(first.dt.offset_by("1mo"), last.dt.offset_by("1mo"))
    .collect()
    .join(factors.select("month", "rf", "market"), on="month", validate="m:1")
    .select("permno", "market", holding="month", excess=100 * pl.col("ret") - pl.col("rf"))
)


def returns_at_horizon(stocks, k):
    realized = (
        stocks.with_columns(holding=pl.col("month").dt.offset_by(f"{k}mo"))
        .drop("month")
        .join(holding_returns, on=["permno", "holding"], validate="1:1")
        .rename({"holding": "month"})
    )
    return portfolio_months(realized, ["portfolio"])

11.4.3 Controlling for Market Capitalization
First divide stocks into five capitalization groups. Then compute mom quintile breakpoints separately within each capitalization group. The last column averages the control portfolios each month before calculating the mean return or estimating an alpha.

from eap_pl import bivariate_months

sort_panel = panel.select(*keys, "mom", "beta", "cap", "bm", "excess", "market")


def two_way_results(
    monthly, weight, control_labels, *, ff_factors=ff3, show_cells=False, show_average=True,
):
    groups = monthly.partition_by("control", as_dict=True)
    series = {label: groups[i,] for i, label in enumerate(control_labels, 1)}
    if show_average:
        series["Average"] = monthly.group_by("month", "target").agg(
            pl.col(weight).mean(), pl.col("market").first(),
        )

    rows = []
    if show_cells:
        for target in range(1, 6):
            rows.append({
                "Statistic": f"`mom` {target}",
                **{label: f'{cell.filter(pl.col("target") == target)[weight].mean():.2f}'
                   for label, cell in series.items()},
            })

    stats = {
        label: spread_statistics(
            spread(cell, 5, 1, "target", weight).with_columns(
                pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo")
            ),
            weight, ff_factors=ff_factors,
        )
        for label, cell in series.items()
    }
    rows.extend({
        "Statistic": f"5–1 {metric}",
        **{label: value[metric] for label, value in stats.items()},
    } for metric in ("Return", "CAPM α", "FF α"))
    return [{"Weights": weights[weight], **row} for row in rows]

11.4.5 Controlling for Beta and Book-to-Market
The dependent sorts calculate mom breakpoints within each beta or bm quintile. The independent sorts use the intersection of two sets of breakpoints computed separately across stocks for each variable. The tables show the high-minus-low mom spread within each control quintile and its average across the control quintiles.

sort_variables = {"beta": "Beta", "cap": "Market cap", "bm": "`bm`"}


def two_way_spreads(pairs, *, dependent, momentum_first=False):
    rows = []
    for control, target in pairs:
        monthly = bivariate_months(sort_panel, control, target, nyse=False, dependent=dependent)
        omit = {"cap": "smb", "bm": "hml"}.get(target)
        ff_factors = [factor for factor in ff3 if factor != omit]
        characteristic = target if momentum_first else control
        for weight in weights:
            rows.extend(
                {"Characteristic": sort_variables[characteristic], **row}
                for row in two_way_results(monthly, weight, quintiles, ff_factors=ff_factors)
            )
    return pl.DataFrame(rows)

title: 11  The Momentum Effect
text:
11.5 The Momentum Factor
The Kenneth French Data Library constructs its momentum factor using six value-weighted portfolios formed on size and prior return. The sorts use an NYSE median for size and NYSE 30th and 70th percentiles for prior return. The factor averages the returns of the small- and large-stock winner portfolios and subtracts the average return of the corresponding loser portfolios. I use the December 2024 release listed in the book’s setup instructions and plot January 1927 through December 2012, the period in BEM.


Code
from io import StringIO
from pathlib import Path
import re

from eap_pl import plot_cumulative_returns

archive = Path("data/momentum-202412.csv").read_text()
monthly_rows = re.findall(r"(?m)^\s*(\d{6},[^\r\n]+)", archive)
momentum_factor = (
    pl.read_csv(
        StringIO("\n".join(monthly_rows)), has_header=False, new_columns=["ym", "mom"],
        schema_overrides={"mom": pl.String},
    )
    .filter(pl.col("ym").is_between(192701, 201212))
    .select(
        date=(pl.col("ym").cast(pl.String) + "01").str.to_date("%Y%m%d"),
        mom=pl.col("mom").str.strip_chars().cast(pl.Float64) / 100,
    )
    .sort("date")
    .with_columns(
        compounded=(1 + pl.col("mom")).cum_prod() - 1,
        cumulative_log=pl.col("mom").log1p().cum_sum(),
    )
)
assert momentum_factor.height == 1032
assert momentum_factor.select(pl.col("mom").is_finite().all()).item()
plot_cumulative_returns(momentum_factor, y_label="Cumulative momentum factor return")








Figure 11.1: Compounded and cumulative log returns of the momentum factor, January 1927–December 2012 (BEM Figure 11.1)





The compounded series shows a sharp drawdown in 2009.

title: 11  The Momentum Effect
text:
11.6 The Fama–French–Carhart Four-Factor Model
Carhart (1997) adds a momentum factor to the three stock-market factors of Fama and French (1993). The four-factor model is BEM’s Equation (11.2).
\[
r_{p,t}=\alpha_p+\beta_{\mathrm{MKT},p}\mathrm{MKT}_t
+\beta_{\mathrm{SMB},p}\mathrm{SMB}_t+\beta_{\mathrm{HML},p}\mathrm{HML}_t
+\beta_{\mathrm{MOM},p}\mathrm{MOM}_t+\varepsilon_{p,t}.
\tag{11.2}\]
Here \(r_{p,t}\) is the excess return of portfolio \(p\), and \(\alpha_p\) is the intercept after accounting for its exposures to the market, size, value, and momentum factors.




Bali, Turan G., Robert F. Engle, and Scott Murray. 2016. Empirical Asset Pricing: The Cross Section of Stock Returns. John Wiley & Sons. https://www.wiley.com/en-us/empirical-asset-pricing-the-cross-section-of-stock-returns-p-9781118095041.


Carhart, Mark M. 1997. “On Persistence in Mutual Fund Performance.” The Journal of Finance 52 (1): 57–82. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1997.tb03808.x.


Fama, Eugene F., and Kenneth R. French. 1993. “Common Risk Factors in the Returns on Stocks and Bonds.” Journal of Financial Economics 33 (1): 3–56. https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-405X(93)90023-5.


Jegadeesh, Narasimhan, and Sheridan Titman. 1993. “Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers: Implications for Stock Market Efficiency.” The Journal of Finance 48 (1): 65–91. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1993.tb04702.x.


Newey, Whitney K., and Kenneth D. West. 1987. “A Simple, Positive Semi-Definite, Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent Covariance Matrix.” Econometrica 55 (3): 703–8. https://doi.org/10.2307/1913610.

title: 12  Short-Term Reversal
text:
12.1 Measuring Short-Term Reversal
Do stocks that rose last month continue to outperform, or do they give back some of their gains? Following Chapter 12 of Bali et al. (2016), I sort on the most recent monthly return and compare its predictive power with that of earlier returns. This complements Chapter 11, where the main momentum signal skips the formation month.
In BEM’s Equation (12.1), the reversal signal is the formation-month CRSP stock return in percentage points.
\[
\operatorname{Rev}_{i,t}=100 R_{i,t}.
\tag{12.1}\]
Here \(R_{i,t}\) is the decimal return for stock \(i\) in month \(t\). Earlier returns are also expressed in percentage points and matched by calendar month, so a gap in the CRSP file does not make an older observation count as the previous month’s return. The formation sample runs from June 1963 through November 2012, and the outcome is the following month’s excess return, including the delisting treatment in Section 7.2.
import polars as pl

from eap_pl import build_book_to_market, build_momentum, build_sizes, load_parquet, monthly_panel

first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)
keys = ["permno", "month"]
lag_labels = {"rev": "`rev`", **{f"lag{k}": f"R(t−{k})" for k in range(1, 12)}}
stock_returns = (
    load_parquet("msf", "crsp")
    .filter(pl.col("date").is_between(first.dt.offset_by("-11mo"), last.dt.month_end()))
    .select(
        "permno", month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start(),
        rev=pl.when(pl.col("ret").is_finite()).then(100 * pl.col("ret")),
    )
)

sizes = build_sizes()
book_to_market = build_book_to_market(sizes).select(*keys, "bm")
panel = (
    monthly_panel(sizes, first, last).lazy()
    .join(book_to_market.lazy(), on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(build_momentum(first, last).select(*keys, "mom").lazy(),
          on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(stock_returns, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
)
for k in range(1, 12):
    lagged = stock_returns.select(
        "permno", month=pl.col("month").dt.offset_by(f"{k}mo"), **{f"lag{k}": pl.col("rev")},
    ).filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first, last))
    panel = panel.join(lagged, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")

panel = panel.collect()

title: 12  Short-Term Reversal
text:
12.3 Reversal and Stock Returns

12.3.1 Univariate Portfolio Analysis
Sort stocks into deciles using breakpoints from all eligible stocks with the signal that month. The value-weighted portfolios use formation-month capitalization. Returns and alphas are in percentage points per month. The high-minus-low spread buys last month’s winners and sells last month’s losers, so a negative spread indicates reversal. I align the factors with the holding month and use the CAPM, the Fama–French three-factor model, and the four-factor model in Equation 11.2. Parentheses show six-lag Newey–West \(t\)-statistics (Newey and West 1987).

from io import StringIO
from pathlib import Path
import re

from eap_pl import format_fit, hac
from eap_pl._portfolios import assign_portfolio, portfolio_months, spread


def archived_factor(filename, name):
    rows = re.findall(r"(?m)^\s*(\d{6},[^\r\n]+)", Path(filename).read_text())
    return (
        pl.read_csv(
            StringIO("\n".join(rows)), has_header=False, new_columns=["ym", name],
            schema_overrides={name: pl.String},
        )
        .select(
            pl.col(name).str.strip_chars().cast(pl.Float64).replace([-99.99, -999], None),
            month=(pl.col("ym").cast(pl.String) + "01").str.to_date("%Y%m%d"),
        )
    )


momentum_factor = archived_factor("data/momentum-202412.csv", "mom_factor")
factors = (
    load_parquet("factors_monthly", "ff")
    .select(
        month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start(),
        mkt=100 * pl.col("mktrf"), smb=100 * pl.col("smb"), hml=100 * pl.col("hml"),
    )
    .collect()
    .join(momentum_factor, on="month", how="left", validate="1:1")
)
models = {
    "Return": "1",
    "CAPM α": "mkt",
    "FF α": "mkt + smb + hml",
    "FFC α": "mkt + smb + hml + mom_factor",
}
weights = {"EW": "Equal weighted", "VW": "Value weighted"}


def portfolio_statistics(series, weight, specifications):
    sample = (
        series.select(pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo"), weight)
        .join(factors, on="month", how="left", validate="m:1")
        .drop_nulls(weight)
        .sort("month")
    )
    return {
        name: format_fit(hac(f"{weight} ~ {rhs}", sample), "Intercept")
        for name, rhs in specifications.items()
    }


characteristics = {"rev": "`rev`", "beta": "Beta", "cap": "Market cap (millions)", "bm": "`bm`", "mom": "`mom`"}
deciles = [str(i) for i in range(1, 11)]
metrics = [pl.col(column).mean().alias(label) for column, label in characteristics.items()]
decile_returns = {}
for term in lag_labels:
    members = assign_portfolio(panel.filter(pl.col(term).is_finite()), term, 10, "month")
    decile_returns[term] = portfolio_months(
        members, ["portfolio"], metrics if term == "rev" else (),
    )



Code
monthly = decile_returns["rev"]
means = monthly.group_by("portfolio").agg(pl.col(*characteristics.values()).mean()).sort("portfolio")
pl.DataFrame([
    {"Characteristic": label, **dict(zip(deciles, means[label]))}
    for label in characteristics.values()
]).eap.show_table()

for weight in weights:
    groups = monthly.partition_by("portfolio", as_dict=True)
    series = {str(i): groups[i,] for i in range(1, 11)}
    series["10–1"] = spread(monthly, 10, 1, "portfolio", weight)
    stats = {label: portfolio_statistics(data, weight, models) for label, data in series.items()}
    pl.DataFrame([
        {"Statistic": name, **{label: values[name] for label, values in stats.items()}}
        for name in models
    ]).eap.show_table()

12.3.3 Controlling for Size, Beta, Book-to-Market, and Momentum
For dependent sorts, calculate reversal breakpoints separately within each control quintile. For independent sorts, calculate both sets of breakpoints for the whole cross-section and intersect the resulting groups. The average column equally weights the control quintiles within each month before estimating the return or alpha.

from eap_pl import bivariate_months

sort_variables = {"beta": "Beta", "cap": "Market cap", "bm": "`bm`", "mom": "`mom`"}
quintiles = [str(i) for i in range(1, 6)]


def two_way_results(monthly, weight, specifications, *, show_cells=False):
    groups = monthly.partition_by("control", as_dict=True)
    series = {label: groups[i,] for i, label in enumerate(quintiles, 1)}
    series["Average"] = monthly.group_by("month", "target").agg(
        pl.col(weight).mean(), pl.col("market").first(),
    )
    rows = []
    if show_cells:
        for target in range(1, 6):
            rows.append({
                "Statistic": f"`rev` {target}",
                **{label: f'{cell.filter(pl.col("target") == target)[weight].mean():.2f}'
                   for label, cell in series.items()},
            })

    stats = {
        label: portfolio_statistics(spread(cell, 5, 1, "target", weight), weight, specifications)
        for label, cell in series.items()
    }
    rows.extend(
        {"Statistic": f"5–1 {name}", **{label: values[name] for label, values in stats.items()}}
        for name in specifications
    )
    return pl.DataFrame(rows)


dependent_sorts = {
    variable: bivariate_months(panel, variable, "rev", nyse=False, dependent=True)
    for variable in sort_variables
}
independent_sorts = {
    variable: bivariate_months(panel, variable, "rev", nyse=False, dependent=False)
    for variable in sort_variables
}

12.3.4 Controlling for Reversal
Now examine beta, size, book-to-market, and momentum spreads within reversal quintiles. For size spreads, omit smb from the factor model. For book-to-market spreads, omit hml. For momentum spreads, use the three-factor model. For the dependent sort, follow BEM’s discussion and the heading of Table 12.8 and set the second breakpoints within each reversal quintile.

def spreads_within_reversal(sorts):
    alpha = {
        "beta": {"FFC α": models["FFC α"]},
        "cap": {"FFC α (excl. `smb`)": "mkt + hml + mom_factor"},
        "bm": {"FFC α (excl. `hml`)": "mkt + smb + mom_factor"},
        "mom": {"FF α": models["FF α"]},
    }
    results = []
    for term, monthly in sorts.items():
        for weight in weights:
            table = two_way_results(monthly, weight, {"Return": "1", **alpha[term]})
            results.append(table.select(
                pl.lit(sort_variables[term]).alias("Second sort"),
                pl.lit(weight).alias("Weights"), pl.all(),
            ))
    return pl.concat(results)

12.5 The Short-Term Reversal Factor
The Kenneth French short-term reversal factor uses six value-weighted portfolios formed by intersecting two size groups and three prior-return groups. The cutoffs are the NYSE median capitalization and the NYSE 30th and 70th percentiles of the previous month’s return. The factor buys recent losers and sells recent winners, so its sign is opposite to the high-minus-low spreads above.
\[
\mathrm{STR}_{t+1}
=\frac{R_{\mathrm{Small,Low},t+1}+R_{\mathrm{Big,Low},t+1}}{2}
-\frac{R_{\mathrm{Small,High},t+1}+R_{\mathrm{Big,High},t+1}}{2}.
\tag{12.2}\]
I use the French library’s December 2024 archive and plot the same July 1926–December 2012 window as BEM. With \(\mathrm{STR}_m\) in decimal units, the two panels use the following scales.
\[
C_t=\prod_{m\le t}(1+\mathrm{STR}_m)-1,
\qquad
L_t=\sum_{m\le t}\log(1+\mathrm{STR}_m).
\tag{12.3}\]


Code
from eap_pl import plot_cumulative_returns

reversal_factor = (
    archived_factor("data/st-reversal-202412.csv", "str")
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(pl.date(1926, 7, 1), pl.date(2012, 12, 1)))
    .rename({"month": "date"})
    .sort("date")
    .with_columns(pl.col("str") / 100)
    .with_columns(
        compounded=(1 + pl.col("str")).cum_prod() - 1,
        cumulative_log=pl.col("str").log1p().cum_sum(),
    )
)
assert reversal_factor["date"].equals(
    pl.date_range(pl.date(1926, 7, 1), pl.date(2012, 12, 1), "1mo", eager=True)
)
assert reversal_factor.select(pl.col("str").is_finite().fill_null(False).all()).item()
plot_cumulative_returns(reversal_factor, y_label="Cumulative reversal factor return")








Figure 12.1: Compounded and cumulative log returns of the short-term reversal factor (BEM Figure 12.1)





The archived series compounds to 121,099% and reaches a cumulative log return of 710.00%.
To estimate the four-factor alpha, use January 1927 through December 2012 because the momentum factor starts in January 1927. The regression outcome is in percentage points per month.

str_sample = (
    reversal_factor.select(month="date", str_pct=100 * pl.col("str"))
    .join(factors.drop_nulls("mom_factor"), on="month", validate="1:1")
    .sort("month")
)
str_fit = hac("str_pct ~ mkt + smb + hml + mom_factor", str_sample)

The four-factor alpha is 0.78% per month (\(t\) = 6.10).

title: 13  Liquidity
text:
13.1 Measuring Illiquidity
Following Chapter 13 of Bali et al. (2016), I ask whether less liquid stocks earn higher subsequent returns. I estimate Amihud illiquidity from legacy CRSP daily data and examine the Pástor–Stambaugh liquidity factors separately. The former measures how much an individual stock’s price moves for a given trading volume. The latter measure marketwide liquidity and exposure to changes in it.
The measure of Amihud (2002) averages the absolute daily return per million dollars traded. For a window of \(k\) calendar months ending in formation month \(t\), let \(\mathcal D_{i,t}^{(k)}\) be the usable trading days and let \(D_{i,t}^{(k)}\) be their count.
\[
\operatorname{Illiq}_{i,t}^{(k)}
=\frac{1}{D_{i,t}^{(k)}}\sum_{d\in\mathcal D_{i,t}^{(k)}}
\frac{|R_{i,d}|}{P_{i,d}Q_{i,d}/10^6}.
\tag{13.1}\]
\(R_{i,d}\) is the decimal CRSP return, \(P_{i,d}\) is the closing trade price, and \(Q_{i,d}\) is the number of shares traded. I require a finite return and strictly positive price and volume. A negative CRSP price denotes a bid–ask average, which BEM exclude for this measure. The minimum counts for the one-, three-, six-, and twelve-month windows are 15, 50, 100, and 200 usable days. I also use \(\log(1+\operatorname{Illiq}_{i,t}^{(k)})\), which reduces the influence of large values without changing their ranks.
import polars as pl

from eap_pl import build_book_to_market, build_momentum, build_sizes, load_parquet, monthly_panel

keys = ["permno", "month"]
first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)
minimum_days = {1: 15, 3: 50, 6: 100, 12: 200}
raw = {f"illiq{k}": f"`illiq{k}`" for k in minimum_days}
logged = {f"log_{term}": f"`log_{term}`" for term in raw}
measures = raw | logged

sizes = build_sizes()
book_to_market = build_book_to_market(sizes).select(*keys, "bm")
stock_months = (
    load_parquet("msf", "crsp")
    .filter(pl.col("date").is_between(first, last.dt.offset_by("1mo").dt.month_end()))
    .select("permno", month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start(),
            stock_return=pl.when(pl.col("ret").is_finite()).then(pl.col("ret")))
)
monthly_factors = (
    load_parquet("factors_monthly", "ff")
    .select("rf", month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start(),
            mkt=100 * pl.col("mktrf"), smb=100 * pl.col("smb"), hml=100 * pl.col("hml"))
    .collect()
)
unadjusted = (
    stock_months.collect()
    .join(monthly_factors.select("month", "rf"), on="month", validate="m:1")
    .select("permno", month=pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("-1mo"),
            unadjusted=100 * (pl.col("stock_return") - pl.col("rf")))
)
formation = (
    monthly_panel(sizes, first, last)
    .join(book_to_market, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(build_momentum(first, last).select(*keys, "mom"), on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(stock_months.select(*keys, rev=100 * pl.col("stock_return")).collect(),
          on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(unadjusted, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
)
Pool the daily ratios and counts over each window so that each usable day receives equal weight. The rolling windows use elapsed calendar months. Months without a usable day contribute zero to the sum and count.
daily = load_parquet("dsf", "crsp").filter(
    pl.col("date").is_between(first.dt.offset_by("-11mo"), last.dt.month_end()),
    pl.col("ret").is_finite(),
    pl.col("prc").is_finite(),
    pl.col("vol").is_finite(),
    pl.col("prc") > 0,
    pl.col("vol") > 0,
)
monthly = (
    daily.with_columns(
        month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start(),
        daily_illiq=pl.col("ret").abs() / (pl.col("prc") * pl.col("vol") / 1e6),
    )
    .group_by(keys)
    .agg(total=pl.col("daily_illiq").sum(), days=pl.len())
    .collect()
    .join(formation.select(keys), on=keys, how="full", coalesce=True, validate="1:1")
    .with_columns(pl.col("total", "days").fill_null(0))
    .sort(keys)
)

panel = formation
for k, minimum in minimum_days.items():
    window = (
        monthly.rolling(index_column="month", period=f"{k}mo", group_by="permno")
        .agg(pl.col("total", "days").sum())
        .select(*keys, pl.when(pl.col("days") >= minimum)
                .then(pl.col("total") / pl.col("days")).alias(f"illiq{k}"))
    )
    panel = panel.join(window, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
panel = panel.with_columns(pl.col(*raw).log1p().name.prefix("log_"))

title: 13  Liquidity
text:
13.3 Illiquidity and Stock Returns
I use next-month excess returns, including the delisting treatment in Section 7.2. One panel of Table 13.4 uses unadjusted CRSP returns to show the effect of including delistings. The risk models are the four-factor model in Equation 11.2 and that model augmented by the short-term reversal factor in Equation 12.2.

from io import StringIO
from pathlib import Path
import re

from eap_pl import format_fit, hac
from eap_pl._portfolios import assign_portfolio, portfolio_months, spread


def archived_factor(filename, name):
    rows = re.findall(r"(?m)^\s*(\d{6},[^\r\n]+)", Path(filename).read_text())
    return (
        pl.read_csv(StringIO("\n".join(rows)), has_header=False,
                    new_columns=["ym", name], schema_overrides={name: pl.String})
        .select(
            pl.col(name).str.strip_chars().cast(pl.Float64).replace([-99.99, -999], None),
            month=(pl.col("ym").cast(pl.String) + "01").str.to_date("%Y%m%d"),
        )
    )


factors = (
    monthly_factors.drop("rf")
    .join(archived_factor("data/momentum-202412.csv", "mom_factor"), on="month", validate="1:1")
    .join(archived_factor("data/st-reversal-202412.csv", "str_factor"), on="month", validate="1:1")
)
ff = "mkt + smb + hml"
ffc = f"{ff} + mom_factor"
ffcstr = f"{ffc} + str_factor"
models = {"Return": "1", "FFC α": ffc, "FFCSTR α": ffcstr}


def factor_fit(series, weight, rhs):
    sample = (
        series.select(pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo"), weight)
        .join(factors, on="month", how="left", validate="1:1")
        .drop_nulls(weight)
        .sort("month")
    )
    return hac(f"{weight} ~ {rhs}", sample)


def spread_statistics(series, weight, specifications):
    return {label: format_fit(factor_fit(series, weight, rhs), "Intercept")
            for label, rhs in specifications.items()}


13.3.1 Univariate Portfolio Analysis
I form monthly deciles using all eligible stocks with each measure, then compute equal- and value-weighted returns. Value weights use formation-month capitalization. The 10–1 portfolio buys the least liquid decile and sells the most liquid decile.

deciles = [str(i) for i in range(1, 11)]
characteristics = {"illiq12": raw["illiq12"], "log_illiq12": logged["log_illiq12"],
                   "beta": "Beta", "cap": "Market cap ($ millions)",
                   "bm": "`bm`", "mom": "`mom`", "rev": "`rev`"}
decile_results = {}
for term in raw:
    members = assign_portfolio(panel.filter(pl.col(term).is_finite()), term, 10, "month")
    metrics = [pl.col("unadjusted").mean().alias("EW unadjusted")]
    if term == "illiq12":
        metrics.extend(pl.col(col).mean().alias(label) for col, label in characteristics.items())
    decile_results[term] = portfolio_months(members, ["portfolio"], metrics)



Code
means = (
    decile_results["illiq12"].group_by("portfolio")
    .agg(pl.col(*characteristics.values()).mean()).sort("portfolio")
)
pl.DataFrame([
    {"Characteristic": label, **dict(zip(deciles, means[label]))}
    for label in characteristics.values()
]).eap.show_table()

for weight in ("EW", "EW unadjusted", "VW"):
    rows = []
    for term, label in raw.items():
        monthly = decile_results[term].rename({weight: "outcome"})
        means = monthly.group_by("portfolio").agg(pl.col("outcome").mean()).sort("portfolio")
        long_short = spread(monthly, 10, 1, "portfolio", "outcome")
        statistics = spread_statistics(long_short, "outcome", models)
        rows.append({"Sort variable": label, **dict(zip(deciles, means["outcome"])),
                     "10–1": statistics.pop("Return"), **statistics})
    pl.DataFrame(rows).eap.show_table()

monthly = decile_results["illiq1"]
groups = monthly.partition_by("portfolio", as_dict=True)
fits = {str(i): factor_fit(groups[i,], "VW", ffcstr) for i in range(1, 11)}
fits["10–1"] = factor_fit(spread(monthly, 10, 1, "portfolio", "VW"), "VW", ffcstr)
terms = {"Intercept": "FFCSTR α", "mkt": "`mkt`", "smb": "`smb`", "hml": "`hml`",
         "mom_factor": "`mom_factor`", "str_factor": "`str_factor`"}
pl.DataFrame([
    {"Statistic": label, **{decile: format_fit(fit, term) for decile, fit in fits.items()}}
    for term, label in terms.items()
]).eap.show_table()

13.3.2 Bivariate Portfolio Analysis
Each two-way sort uses stocks with both characteristics available. I form quintiles first on a control variable, then on twelve-month illiquidity. In dependent sorts, I calculate the second set of cutoffs within each control quintile. In independent sorts, I calculate both sets of cutoffs from the monthly cross-section and intersect the groups. The average column weights the available control cells equally within each month and illiquidity quintile.

from eap_pl import bivariate_months

quintiles = [f"Q{i}" for i in range(1, 6)]
group_labels = [*quintiles, "Average"]


def spread_by_control(monthly, weight):
    groups = monthly.partition_by("control", as_dict=True)
    averaged = monthly.group_by("month", "target").agg(
        pl.col(weight).mean(), pl.col("market").first(),
    )
    return {
        label: spread(group, 5, 1, "target", weight)
        for label, group in zip(group_labels, [*(groups[i,] for i in range(1, 6)), averaged])
    }


def two_way_spreads(pairs, dependent, model_overrides=None):
    model_overrides = model_overrides or {}
    rows = []
    for control, target, label in pairs:
        sample = panel.filter(pl.all_horizontal(pl.col(control, target).is_finite()))
        monthly = bivariate_months(sample, control, target, nyse=False, dependent=dependent)
        specifications = model_overrides.get(target, models)
        for weight in ("EW", "VW"):
            spreads = {group: spread_statistics(series, weight, specifications)
                       for group, series in spread_by_control(monthly, weight).items()}
            for statistic in specifications:
                rows.append({"Characteristic": label, "Weights": weight, "Statistic": statistic,
                             **{group: values[statistic] for group, values in spreads.items()}})
    return pl.DataFrame(rows)

size_sample = panel.filter(pl.all_horizontal(pl.col("cap", "illiq12").is_finite()))
size_groups = assign_portfolio(size_sample, "cap", 5, "month", label="control")
size_groups = assign_portfolio(size_groups, "illiq12", 5, ["month", "control"], label="target")
size_cells = portfolio_months(
    size_groups.drop_nulls(["control", "target"]), ["control", "target"],
    [pl.col("cap").mean().alias("size")],
)


def size_grid(value):
    grid = (
        size_cells.group_by("target", "control").agg(pl.col(value).mean())
        .with_columns(group=pl.format("Q{}", pl.col("control")))
        .pivot(on="group", index="target", values=value)
    )
    month_averages = (
        size_cells.group_by("month", "target").agg(pl.col(value).mean())
        .group_by("target").agg(pl.col(value).mean().alias("Average"))
    )
    return (
        grid.join(month_averages, on="target", validate="1:1")
        .sort("target")
        .select(pl.format("`illiq12` {}", pl.col("target")).alias("Portfolio"), *group_labels)
    )


size_spreads = {group: spread_statistics(series, "EW", models)
                for group, series in spread_by_control(size_cells, "EW").items()}
return_rows = [
    {"Portfolio": label, **{group: f"{value:.2f}" for group, value in zip(group_labels, values)}}
    for label, *values in size_grid("EW").iter_rows()
]
return_rows.extend(
    {"Portfolio": f"5–1 {statistic}", **{group: result[statistic] for group, result in size_spreads.items()}}
    for statistic in models
)
pl.DataFrame(return_rows).eap.show_table()
size_grid("size").with_columns(pl.col(group_labels).round().cast(pl.Int64)).eap.show_table()

13.3.3 Fama–MacBeth Regressions
I regress subsequent excess returns on the formation-month characteristics separately each month. For each specification I keep complete cases before winsorizing the regressors at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles within month. I use six-lag Newey–West standard errors for the average coefficients. The raw and log illiquidity measures produce the same ranks but need not produce the same regression results.

    return tables[0].select("Term").with_columns(
        table["(1)"].alias(f"({i})") for i, table in enumerate(tables, 1)
    )

title: 13  Liquidity
text:
13.4 Liquidity Factors
The stock-level liquidity measure of Pástor and Stambaugh (2003) captures the following day’s reversal after trading pressure. For each stock and month they estimate
\[
r_{i,d+1}-r_{M,d+1}
=\theta_{i,m}+\phi_{i,m}r_{i,d}
+\gamma_{i,m}\operatorname{sign}(r_{i,d}-r_{M,d})V_{i,d}
+\varepsilon_{i,d+1},
\tag{13.2}\]
where \(V_{i,d}\) is dollar volume in millions and both days fall in month \(m\). The fit requires at least 15 usable pairs. A more negative \(\widehat{\gamma}_{i,m}\) associates signed volume with a larger subsequent reversal.
The aggregate measure averages the estimated stock coefficients for the eligible stocks.
\[
\widehat{\gamma}_m=\frac{1}{N_m}\sum_{i=1}^{N_m}\widehat{\gamma}_{i,m}.
\tag{13.3}\]
The aggregation uses stocks with a price of $5 to $1,000 at the prior month-end. The plotted level scales the average by \(V_m/V_1\), using the total prior month-end capitalization of the eligible stocks and August 1962 as the base month. I use the authors’ December 2013 release, the same vintage used by BEM. The file comes with eap_pl and includes the aggregate level, innovations, and traded factor.

from plotnine_polars import aes

from eap_pl import load_pastor_stambaugh_2013

end = pl.date(2012, 12, 1)
liquidity = load_pastor_stambaugh_2013().filter(pl.col("date") <= end)
assert liquidity["date"].equals(pl.date_range(pl.date(1962, 8, 1), end, "1mo", eager=True))
assert liquidity.select(pl.all_horizontal(pl.col("level", "innovation").is_finite()).fill_null(False).all()).item()


def plot_liquidity(series, label):
    return (
        liquidity.ggplot(aes(x="date", y=series))
        .geom_hline(yintercept=0, color="#777777", size=0.45)
        .geom_line(color="#15627c", size=0.55)
        .scale_x_date(date_breaks="10 years", date_labels="%Y")
        .labs(x="Month", y=label)
        .theme_minimal()
        .add_theme(figure_size=(8.2, 3.25))
    )



Code
plot_liquidity("level", "Aggregate liquidity")








Figure 13.1: Scaled aggregate market liquidity, August 1962 to December 2012 (BEM Figure 13.1)





To isolate liquidity innovations, Pástor and Stambaugh average the change in stock-level liquidity among stocks observed in both months and scale it by market capitalization for that set of stocks.
\[
\Delta\widehat{\gamma}_m =
\frac{V_m}{V_1}\frac{1}{N_m}
\sum_{i=1}^{N_m}(\widehat{\gamma}_{i,m}-\widehat{\gamma}_{i,m-1}).
\tag{13.4}\]
\[
\Delta\widehat{\gamma}_m =
a+b\,\Delta\widehat{\gamma}_{m-1}
+c\,\frac{V_{m-1}}{V_1}\widehat{\gamma}_{m-1}+u_m.
\tag{13.5}\]
\[
L_m=\frac{\widehat u_m}{100}.
\tag{13.6}\]


Code
plot_liquidity("innovation", "Liquidity innovation")








Figure 13.2: Innovations in aggregate market liquidity, August 1962 to December 2012 (BEM Figure 13.2)





The traded factor compares stocks with high and low historical exposure to liquidity innovations. Pástor and Stambaugh estimate the exposure \(\beta_{i,L}\) from up to five years of monthly excess returns, requiring at least 36 observations.
\[
r_{i,m}^{e}=\alpha_i+\beta_{i,M}\mathrm{MKT}_m+
\beta_{i,S}\mathrm{SMB}_m+\beta_{i,H}\mathrm{HML}_m+
\beta_{i,L}L_m+\varepsilon_{i,m}.
\tag{13.7}\]
At portfolio formation, the innovations used in this regression are estimated with data available at that date. The liquidity betas are updated at year-end and used during the following calendar year. The factor is the value-weighted return on the highest liquidity-beta decile minus the return on the lowest. I compound the published monthly factor returns beginning in January 1968 and also sum their log returns as in Equation 12.3.

assert traded.select((pl.col("psl").is_finite() & (pl.col("psl") > -1)).fill_null(False).all()).item()

title: 14  Skewness
text:
14.1 Measuring Skewness
Following Chapter 14 of Bali et al. (2016), I measure the asymmetry of past stock returns and ask whether it predicts next month’s return. I examine total skewness, exposure to large market moves, and skewness in the residuals from a factor model.
Total skewness is the third central moment of raw stock returns divided by the second central moment raised to the power \(3/2\). If \(R_{i,s}\) is a return for stock \(i\) and \(\bar R_i\) is its mean in the estimation window, then
\[
\operatorname{Skew}_i=
\frac{n^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{n}(R_{i,s}-\bar R_i)^3}
{\left[n^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{n}(R_{i,s}-\bar R_i)^2\right]^{3/2}}.
\tag{14.1}\]
I use the moment formula as written. A constant return series has no defined total skewness.
Co-skewness is the coefficient on the squared market excess return in a regression of stock excess returns.
\[
r_{i,s}=\alpha_i+\beta_i\mathrm{MKT}_s+
\operatorname{CoSkew}_i\mathrm{MKT}_s^2+\varepsilon_{i,s}.
\tag{14.2}\]
The coefficient depends on the units of return. I fit the regression with decimal returns throughout.
Idiosyncratic skewness applies the same moment ratio to mean-zero residuals.
\[
\operatorname{IdioSkew}_i=
\frac{n^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{n}\hat\varepsilon_{i,s}^{\,3}}
{\left[n^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{n}\hat\varepsilon_{i,s}^{\,2}\right]^{3/2}}.
\tag{14.3}\]
The residuals come from the Fama–French three-factor regression.
\[
r_{i,s}=\alpha_i+\beta_{i,M}\mathrm{MKT}_s+
\beta_{i,S}\mathrm{SMB}_s+\beta_{i,H}\mathrm{HML}_s+\varepsilon_{i,s}.
\tag{14.4}\]
The formation months are June 1963 through November 2012. The daily windows cover 1, 3, 6, or 12 calendar months and require 15, 50, 100, or 200 observations, respectively. The monthly windows cover 1, 2, 3, or 5 years and require 10, 20, 24, or 24 observations. All windows end in the formation month. The factor regressions match returns to factors at the same frequency and use observations with all the inputs required for that regression. I use the June 2014 archive for the daily and monthly Fama–French factors and the monthly momentum factor.
import polars as pl

from eap_pl import (
    build_book_to_market, build_momentum, build_sizes, get_ff_factors, load_parquet, monthly_panel,
)
from eap_pl._skewness import rolling_skewness

first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)
keys = ["permno", "month"]
daily_windows = {"1m": (1, 15), "3m": (3, 50), "6m": (6, 100), "12m": (12, 200)}
monthly_windows = {"1y": (12, 10), "2y": (24, 20), "3y": (36, 24), "5y": (60, 24)}
windows = daily_windows | monthly_windows

vintage = "201406"
daily_factors = get_ff_factors("daily", vintage=vintage)
monthly_factors = get_ff_factors("monthly", vintage=vintage)

sizes = build_sizes()
monthly_stocks = (
    load_parquet("msf", "crsp")
    .filter(pl.col("date").is_between(first.dt.offset_by("-59mo"), last.dt.month_end()))
    .select("permno", "ret", date=pl.col("date").dt.month_start())
)
formation = (
    monthly_panel(sizes, first, last, monthly_factors=monthly_factors)
    .join(build_book_to_market(sizes).select(*keys, "bm"), on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(build_momentum(first, last).select(*keys, "mom"), on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    .join(monthly_stocks.select(
        "permno", month="date", rev=pl.when(pl.col("ret").is_finite()).then(100 * pl.col("ret")),
    ).collect(), on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
)
anchors = formation.select(keys)
daily_stocks = load_parquet("dsf", "crsp").filter(
    pl.col("date").is_between(first.dt.offset_by("-11mo"), last.dt.month_end()),
)

daily_measures = rolling_skewness(anchors, daily_stocks, daily_factors, daily_windows)
monthly_measures = rolling_skewness(anchors, monthly_stocks, monthly_factors, monthly_windows)
I also need the one-month Amihud illiquidity control from Chapter 13. It averages absolute returns per million dollars traded across at least 15 valid days.
illiq = (
    daily_stocks.filter(
        pl.col("date") >= first,
        pl.all_horizontal(pl.col("ret", "prc", "vol").is_finite()),
        pl.col("prc") > 0,
        pl.col("vol") > 0,
    )
    .with_columns(month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start())
    .group_by(keys)
    .agg(illiq=(1e6 * pl.col("ret").abs() / (pl.col("prc") * pl.col("vol"))).mean(),
         days=pl.len())
    .filter(pl.col("days") >= 15)
    .select(*keys, "illiq")
    .collect()
)
panel = (
    formation.join(daily_measures, on=keys, validate="1:1")
    .join(monthly_measures, on=keys, validate="1:1")
    .join(illiq, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
)
families = {"skew": "Total skewness", "coskew": "Co-skewness", "idioskew": "Idiosyncratic skewness"}
labels = {
    family: {f"{family}_{horizon}": f"`{family}_{horizon}`" for horizon in windows}
    for family in families
}
controls = {"beta": "Beta", "log_cap": "Size", "bm": "`bm`",
            "mom": "`mom`", "rev": "`rev`", "illiq": "`illiq`"}

14.3 Correlations
I calculate Pearson and Spearman correlations within each month on observations where both measures are available. For Pearson correlations I winsorize each variable at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles. Spearman correlations use the original ranks.

from itertools import combinations

from eap_pl import correlation_matrix, period_correlations, winsorized_corr


def within_family(family):
    terms = labels[family]
    means = (
        period_correlations(panel, terms, "month")
        .select(pl.exclude("month").mean())
        .row(0, named=True)
    )
    return correlation_matrix(means, terms)

The next two tables compare different types of skewness over the same window, then relate each measure to beta, size, book-to-market, momentum, reversal, and illiquidity.

def average_pairs(pairs):
    expressions = []
    for left, right in pairs:
        a, b = pl.col(left), pl.col(right)
        valid = pl.all_horizontal(a.is_finite(), b.is_finite())
        expressions.extend([
            winsorized_corr(a, b).alias(f"Pearson {left} {right}"),
            pl.corr(a.filter(valid), b.filter(valid), method="spearman").alias(f"Spearman {left} {right}"),
        ])
    return (
        panel.group_by("month").agg(expressions)
        .select(pl.exclude("month").fill_nan(None).mean())
        .row(0, named=True)
    )

14.4 Persistence
I pair a stock’s current measure with its value an exact number of months later. I compute the winsorized Pearson correlation across those paired stocks each month, then average across months. I omit lags shorter than the estimation window because the two measures would share returns.

from eap_pl import persistence

lags = [1, 3, 6, 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 120]


def nonoverlapping_persistence(family):
    terms = labels[family]
    return persistence(panel, terms, lags).with_columns(
        pl.when(pl.col("Lag (months)") >= months)
        .then(pl.col(terms[f"{family}_{window}"])).alias(terms[f"{family}_{window}"])
        for window, (months, _) in windows.items()
    )

title: 15  Idiosyncratic Volatility
text:
15.1 Measuring Total Volatility
I follow Chapter 15 of Bali et al. (2016). I examine whether stocks with more volatile factor-model residuals earn lower returns in the next month, and how the relation changes with portfolio weighting, delisting adjustments, and controls.
Let \(R_{i,s}\) be a decimal stock return, \(n\) the number of observations in the estimation window, and \(m\) the number of periods per year. I use \(m=252\) for daily returns and \(m=12\) for monthly returns. Total volatility is the annualized sample standard deviation, in percent.
\[
\operatorname{Vol}_i = 100\sqrt{m}\,\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{s=1}^{n}(R_{i,s}-\bar R_i)^2}{n-1}}.
\tag{15.1}\]
I also calculate an annualized root mean square using zero in place of the sample mean.
\[
\operatorname{Vol}^{SS}_i = 100\sqrt{m}\,\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{s=1}^{n}R_{i,s}^2}{n}}.
\tag{15.2}\]
crumbs: Part II. The Cross Section of Stock Returns

title: 15  Idiosyncratic Volatility
text:
15.2 Measuring Idiosyncratic Volatility
I regress the stock return in excess of the risk-free rate, \(r_{i,s}\), on factor returns at the same frequency. The Fama–French three-factor model uses market, size, and value returns.
\[
r_{i,s}=\alpha_i+\beta_{i,M}\mathrm{MKT}_s+\beta_{i,S}\mathrm{SMB}_s
+\beta_{i,H}\mathrm{HML}_s+\varepsilon_{i,s}.
\tag{15.3}\]
The CAPM uses the market factor.
\[
r_{i,s}=\alpha_i+\beta_{i,M}\mathrm{MKT}_s+\varepsilon_{i,s}.
\tag{15.4}\]
The four-factor model (FFC) adds momentum.
\[
r_{i,s}=\alpha_i+\beta_{i,M}\mathrm{MKT}_s+\beta_{i,S}\mathrm{SMB}_s
+\beta_{i,H}\mathrm{HML}_s+\beta_{i,U}\mathrm{MOM}_s+\varepsilon_{i,s}.
\tag{15.5}\]
Let \(k\) denote the number of estimated coefficients, including the intercept. Here \(k\) equals 4 for FF, 2 for CAPM, and 5 for FFC.
\[
\operatorname{RSE}_i=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{s=1}^{n}\widehat\varepsilon_{i,s}^{2}}{n-k}}.
\tag{15.6}\]
Idiosyncratic volatility annualizes the residual standard error and expresses it in percent.
\[
\operatorname{IdioVol}_i=100\sqrt{m}\,\operatorname{RSE}_i.
\tag{15.7}\]
Formation months run from June 1963 through November 2012. Each window ends in the formation month. The daily windows of 1, 3, 6, and 12 months require 15, 50, 100, and 200 observations. The monthly windows of 1, 2, 3, and 5 years require 10, 20, 24, and 24 observations. For factor models, the minimum applies to matched observations. I use CRSP’s reported stock returns to estimate volatility and download the June 2014 vintage of the factors, including daily momentum, with get_ff_factors().

import polars as pl

from eap_pl import get_ff_factors, load_beta_universe, load_monthly_betas, load_parquet, ptime
from eap_pl._volatility import rolling_volatility

first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)
last_holding = last.dt.offset_by("1mo")
keys = ["permno", "month"]
daily_windows = {"1m": (1, 15), "3m": (3, 50), "6m": (6, 100), "12m": (12, 200)}
monthly_windows = {"1y": (12, 10), "2y": (24, 20), "3y": (36, 24), "5y": (60, 24)}
windows = daily_windows | monthly_windows

anchors = load_beta_universe(first, last).sort(keys).collect()
daily = load_parquet("dsf", "crsp").filter(
    pl.col("date").is_between(first.dt.offset_by("-11mo"), last.dt.month_end())
)
monthly = (
    load_parquet("msf", "crsp")
    .filter(pl.col("date").is_between(first.dt.offset_by("-59mo"), last_holding.dt.month_end()))
    .select("permno", "ret", date=pl.col("date").dt.month_start())
    .with_columns(pl.when(pl.col("ret").is_finite()).then("ret").alias("ret"))
)

vintage = "201406"
daily_factors = get_ff_factors("daily", vintage=vintage).join(
    get_ff_factors("momentum_daily", vintage=vintage), on="date", how="left", validate="1:1"
)
monthly_factors = get_ff_factors("monthly", vintage=vintage).join(
    get_ff_factors("momentum", vintage=vintage), on="date", how="left", validate="1:1"
)

with ptime():
    daily_vol = rolling_volatility(anchors, daily, daily_factors, daily_windows, 252)

Wall time: 24.465 s



with ptime():
    monthly_vol = rolling_volatility(anchors, monthly, monthly_factors, monthly_windows, 12)

I use the 12-month daily market beta, one-month Amihud illiquidity from Chapter 13, and the five-year monthly co-skewness and idiosyncratic skewness measures from Chapter 14. I use log market capitalization (log_cap), the cumulative return over the preceding 11 months (mom), and the formation-month return (rev) as controls.

from eap_pl import build_book_to_market, build_momentum, build_sizes
from eap_pl._data import monthly_stock_returns
from eap_pl._skewness import rolling_skewness

with ptime():
    usable_days = daily.filter(
        pl.all_horizontal(pl.col("ret", "prc", "vol").is_finite()),
        pl.col("prc") > 0,
        pl.col("vol") > 0,
    ).with_columns(month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start())

    illiquidity = (
        usable_days.filter(pl.col("month") >= first)
        .group_by(keys)
        .agg(illiq=(1e6 * pl.col("ret").abs() / (pl.col("prc") * pl.col("vol"))).mean(),
             days=pl.len())
        .filter(pl.col("days") >= 15)
        .select(*keys, "illiq")
        .collect()
    )

    skewness = rolling_skewness(anchors, monthly, monthly_factors, {"5y": monthly_windows["5y"]})
    sizes = build_sizes()
    betas = load_monthly_betas(first, last)
    adjusted = monthly_stock_returns(first.dt.offset_by("1mo"), last_holding).rename({"ret": "adjusted"})
    holding_returns = (
        monthly.select("permno", month="date", unadjusted="ret")
        .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first.dt.offset_by("1mo"), last_holding))
        .join(adjusted, on=keys, how="full", coalesce=True, validate="1:1")
        .join(monthly_factors.lazy().select("rf", month="date", market=100 * pl.col("mktrf")),
              on="month", validate="m:1")
        .select("permno", pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("-1mo"), "market",
                excess=100 * (pl.col("adjusted") - pl.col("rf")),
                raw_excess=100 * (pl.col("unadjusted") - pl.col("rf")))
        .collect()
    )

    panel = (
        volatility.join(skewness.select(*keys, "coskew_5y", "idioskew_5y"), on=keys, validate="1:1")
        .join(betas, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
        .join(sizes.select(*keys, "cap", "log_cap"), on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
        .join(build_book_to_market(sizes).select(*keys, "bm"), on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
        .join(build_momentum(first, last).select(*keys, "mom"), on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
        .join(monthly.select("permno", month="date", rev=100 * pl.col("ret")).collect(),
              on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
        .join(illiquidity, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
        .join(holding_returns, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")

text:
15.4 Correlations
Within each formation month, I use stocks with both measures available and winsorize each variable at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles. Each table averages the resulting correlations across months. The square tables put Pearson coefficients below the diagonal and Spearman coefficients above it.

from itertools import combinations

from eap_pl import correlation_matrix


def average_pairs(pairs):
    expressions = []
    for left, right in pairs:
        a, b = pl.col(left), pl.col(right)
        valid = pl.all_horizontal(a.is_finite(), b.is_finite())
        a, b = (x.filter(valid).eap.winsorize(prob=0.005, quantile_method="linear")
                for x in (a, b))
        expressions.extend([
            pl.corr(a, b).alias(f"Pearson {left}–{right}"),
            pl.corr(a, b, method="spearman").alias(f"Spearman {left}–{right}"),
        ])
    return (
        panel.group_by("month").agg(expressions)
        .select(pl.exclude("month").fill_nan(None).mean()).row(0, named=True)
    )


def within_family(family):
    terms = labels[family]
    return correlation_matrix(average_pairs(combinations(terms, 2)), terms)

title: 16  Liquid Samples
text:
16.1 Screens
Following Chapter 16 of Bali et al. (2016), I examine how price and size screens change the distribution of stock characteristics and their relation to future returns. I use June 1963 through November 2012 as formation months and July 1963 through December 2012 as holding months.
The CRSP sample consists of US common stocks. Let \(P_{i,t}\) be the absolute value of the month-end alternate price (altprc), \(C_{i,t}\) the month-end market capitalization, and \(q_{0.10,t}^{\mathrm{NYSE}}\) the 10th percentile of capitalization among NYSE common stocks in the full CRSP sample. The screens are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal P_t &= \{i\in\mathcal U_t : 5 \le P_{i,t} \le 1000\},\\
\mathcal S_t &= \{i\in\mathcal P_t : C_{i,t} \ge q_{0.10,t}^{\mathrm{NYSE}}\},
\end{aligned}
\tag{16.1}\]
where \(\mathcal U_t\) is the CRSP sample in month \(t\). The price screen uses nominal dollars. Compute the NYSE breakpoint before applying the price screen.
import polars as pl

from eap_pl import (
    build_book_to_market, build_momentum, build_sizes, get_ff_factors,
    load_parquet, monthly_panel, ptime, rolling_ols,
)
from eap_pl._skewness import rolling_skewness

first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)
keys = ["permno", "month"]
vintage = "201406"
daily_factors = get_ff_factors("daily", vintage=vintage)
monthly_factors = get_ff_factors("monthly", vintage=vintage)
monthly = (
    load_parquet("msf", "crsp")
    .filter(pl.col("date").is_between(first.dt.offset_by("-59mo"), last.dt.month_end()))
    .select("permno", "ret", date=pl.col("date").dt.month_start(), price=pl.col("altprc").abs())
)
daily = (
    load_parquet("dsf", "crsp")
    .filter(pl.col("date").is_between(first, last.dt.month_end()))
    .select("permno", "date", "ret", "prc", "vol")
)
The characteristic definitions follow the preceding chapters. I use the 12-month daily beta, one-month Amihud illiquidity, five-year monthly co-skewness and idiosyncratic skewness, and one-month daily Fama–French idiosyncratic volatility. Size is the natural logarithm of nominal market capitalization in millions of dollars. Next-month excess returns include the delisting adjustments described in Section 7.2.
with ptime():
    sizes = build_sizes()
    formation = (
        monthly_panel(sizes.select(*keys, "cap", "log_cap", "exchcd"), first, last,
                      monthly_factors=monthly_factors)
        .join(build_book_to_market(sizes).select(*keys, "bm"), on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
        .join(build_momentum(first, last).select(*keys, "mom"), on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
        .join(monthly.select(
            "permno", "price", month="date",
            rev=pl.when(pl.col("ret").is_finite()).then(100 * pl.col("ret")),
        ).collect(), on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
    )
    anchors = formation.select(keys)
    illiquidity = (
        daily.filter(
            pl.all_horizontal(pl.col("ret", "prc", "vol").is_finite()),
            pl.col("prc") > 0,
            pl.col("vol") > 0,
        )
        .with_columns(month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start())
        .group_by(keys)
        .agg(illiq=(1e6 * pl.col("ret").abs() / (pl.col("prc") * pl.col("vol"))).mean(),
             days=pl.len())
        .filter(pl.col("days") >= 15)
        .select(*keys, "illiq")
        .collect()
    )
    skew = rolling_skewness(anchors, monthly, monthly_factors, {"5y": (60, 24)})
    daily_excess = (
        daily.join(daily_factors.lazy(), on="date", how="left", validate="m:1")
        .with_columns(excess=pl.col("ret") - pl.col("rf"))
    )
    idio = rolling_ols(daily_excess, y="excess", x=["mktrf", "smb", "hml"],
                       group_by="permno", date_col="date", anchors=anchors,
                       months=1, min_obs=15).select(
        *keys, idio_vol=pl.col("rmse") * (100 * 252**0.5),
    )
    panel = (
        formation.join(illiquidity, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
        .join(skew.select(*keys, "coskew_5y", "idioskew_5y"), on=keys, validate="1:1")
        .join(idio, on=keys, validate="1:1")
    )

nyse_cutoff = (
    panel.filter((pl.col("exchcd") == 1) & pl.col("cap").is_finite())
    .group_by("month").agg(cutoff=pl.col("cap").quantile(0.1, interpolation="linear"))
)
price_sample = panel.filter(pl.col("price").is_finite() & pl.col("price").is_between(5, 1000))
size_sample = (
    price_sample.join(nyse_cutoff, on="month", validate="m:1")
    .filter(pl.col("cap").is_finite() & (pl.col("cap") >= pl.col("cutoff")))
)
samples = {"CRSP": panel, "Price": price_sample, "Size": size_sample}

text:
16.5 Fama–MacBeth Regressions
For each sample, I estimate the monthly cross-sectional regression
\[
r_{i,t+1} = a_t + \mathbf{x}_{i,t}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{b}_t + \varepsilon_{i,t+1}.
\tag{16.3}\]
I fit a separate univariate regression for each characteristic and one regression with all nine characteristics. Within each specification, I winsorize regressors at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles among that month’s complete cases. I report the time-series averages of the coefficients, adjusted \(R^2\), and sample size, with six-lag Newey–West t-statistics on the average coefficients.

from eap_pl import fama_macbeth_table

def regression_tables(sample):
    univariate = {}
    for term, label in regressors.items():
        fit = fama_macbeth_table(
            sample.drop_nulls(["excess", term]), [[term]], {term: label}, digits=3,
        )
        univariate[label] = fit["(1)"]
    terms = list(regressors)
    full_fit = fama_macbeth_table(
        sample.drop_nulls(["excess", *terms]), [terms], regressors, digits=3,
    )
    values = dict(full_fit.iter_rows())
    headers = ["Intercept", *regressors.values(), "Adjusted R²", "n"]
    return [
        pl.DataFrame({"Statistic": ["Slope", "Intercept", "Adjusted R²", "n"], **univariate}),
        pl.DataFrame({label: [values[label]] for label in headers}),
    ]

with ptime():
    regressions = [table for sample in samples.values() for table in regression_tables(sample)]
